The 11th Plenary Meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Teiti Maamao, President and Minister for Foreign Affairs and Immigration of the Republic of Kiribati. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, Distinguished Heads of States and Governments, Ladies and Gentlemen, In the name of Almighty God in whom we place our trust, Kamnabeni Nimaudi. On behalf of the Government and the people of Kiribati, I extend our warmest congratulations to you, Mr. President, on your election to preside and lead this 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Kiribati assures you of our full support and cooperation as you undertake this important responsibility. Mr. President, we meet today at a difficult moment. Conflicts continue to claim lives and displace communities. Human rights continue to be violated. Humanitarian crises persist. Development gains are being reversed in many parts of the world. Inequality remains entrenched, while climate change places additional pressure on communities already confronting significant development challenges. It is therefore fitting that the theme of this 81st session is "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all". This theme is both timely and relevant. Trust cannot be restored by words alone. It must be strengthened through implementation, accountability and results that improve the lives of our people. For Kiribati, the theme reaffirms our shared duty to strengthen the United Nations and ensure it serves everyone. Mr. President, Kiribati is an ocean nation. We are a big ocean sustainable state. Our economy, food security, livelihoods, culture, and the way of life depend on healthy, sustainable marine resources. Sustainable management is essential to our long-term developments, and we call for increased efforts and partnerships to have agreeable progress towards SDG 14, which is conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas, and marine resources for sustainable development. The 2026 Sustainable Development Goals reports reminds us that our oceans and fisheries continue to face mounting pressures from overfishing, illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, pollution, warming, and acidification. The entry into force of the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Agreement marks an important step towards stronger, and more equitable ocean governance. Kiribati is proud to have signed and ratified this agreement and calls on member states to recognize the vital importance of our shared oceans and to work collectively to translate the agreement's historic ambition into meaningful global action. Mr. President, The sustainability of our ocean and fisheries is closely linked to the changing climate and the pressures we face on our marine resources are increasingly compounded by its impact. Climate remains one of the most pressing challenges to our development and the way of life. Sea level rise, coastal erosion, South water intrusion and extreme. weather events continue to place pressure on our communities, infrastructure, water security and livelihoods. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report reinforces the urgency of these challenges, and particularly the risk faced by small island states. Through our long-term national development mission, the GIDA vision for 20 years, our national priorities, and the Tamusindano policies, we continue to invest in resilience infrastructure, water security, coastal protection, disaster preparedness, renewable energy, and community-based adaptation. Our objective is clear. to continue building a wealthy, healthy, and peaceful Kiribati, where our people can live with dignity, in peace, and with opportunities. Renewable energy is increasingly important to Kiribati's development and energy access. We therefore see greater investment in renewable energy as an important opportunity. to reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the resilience and sustainability of our energy sector. But national action must be matched by international action. We call for greater ambition, stronger support for adaptation and climate finance that is adequate, predictable, and accessible. particularly for small island developing states. Kiribati recognizes the importance of international law in addressing climate change. The International Court of Justice advisory opinion on climate change advances climate justice by affirming that all states have binding duties to protect the climate system and achieve deep, rapid, and sustained greenhouse gas reductions consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. We welcome growing recognition that climate resilience must be locally owned and driven. The Pacific Resilience Facility is a Pacific-led, Pacific-owned mechanism that strengthens the region's capacity to finance climate and disaster resilience. The Pacific's co-hosting of COP31 with Turkey later this year further demonstrates the value of local action. These initiatives also show that strong, genuine partnerships can sustain locally-led development. Mr. President, Partnership continues to shape international cooperation as we believe that we are stronger when we work together. At a time when multilateralism faces growing challenges, partnership remains one of our most powerful affirmations of what we can achieve collectively. Kiribati reaffirms its support for frameworks that embody the spirit of partnership including the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Cities, ABAF, and the Pacific for the Future, which provide important foundations for strengthened international cooperation, solidarity, and collective action. As the 2030 Agenda enters its final years, partnership must remain central to accelerating SDG progress. Guatemala recently presented its second Voluntary National Review, reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 agenda. We value our long-standing diplomatic relations with traditional partners and welcome countries seeking new partnerships. based on mutual respect, shared interest, transparency, sovereign equality, and respect for our national priorities. This year, following the submission of our second VNR, my government convened its first Development Partners Forum on Christmas Island, which we highly value as the world's largest coral atoll and the first island to see each new day's sunrise. This forum strengthened partnerships between Kiribati and its development partners and showcased two flagship projects critical to accelerating economic growth and sustainable development. Participants included Australia, the People's Republic of China, the European Union, New Zealand, Japan, the United States of America, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and the UN agencies. We thank our partners and look forward to advancing our shared interests under the forum's outcome documents we call the Christmas Partnership Accord 2026. Mr. President, ultimately, development depends on people, our most valuable resource. Making education a vital investment, Kiribati is committed to expanding access to quality, inclusive, relevant education while strengthening skills development skills development, vocational training, digital learning, and opportunities for young people. Health is equally fundamental. We continue to strengthen our health systems across our widely dispersed and remote islands, improve access to essential services, and address both communicable and non-communicable diseases. Healthy An educated population is the foundation upon which every other national priority rests. Mr. President, we cannot speak about development without speaking about women and youth. Kiribati remains committed to gender equality and empowering women and girls. Our election earlier this year to the Commission on the Status of Women, the first time Kiribati has secured a seat on this UN body, is a significant milestone, reflecting our determination to advance women's rights nationally and globally. We will expand opportunities, prevent violence, and promote women's economic empowerment and leadership. Our youth Meanwhile, represent not simply the future of Kiribati. We must provide them with education, employment, skills, technology, leadership opportunities, and spaces where they can contribute. And one of those spaces is sports. Kiribati will host the 2030 Micronesian Games, which we intend to use to leave a lasting legacy for our young people. We invite our regional and international partners to join us in this endeavor. For Kiribati, on peace and security. Mr. President, Kiribati is a peaceful nation. Yet, distance does not make a difference to the suffering caused by war and conflicts elsewhere. The people of every nation deserve peace. We reaffirm that disputes must be resolved peacefully, in accordance with the international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter. For island nations such as Kiribati, Respect for international law is fundamental to our security, sovereignty, and stability of the international system. Kiribati is proud to contribute in our own way to international peace and security through the service of our police officers under the United Nations flag. For Kiribati, This is an expression of our belief that even the smallest country can contribute to global peace. For Pacific people, the consequences of nuclear weapons are not merely historical. Our region bears the human and environmental legacy of nuclear testing. As state parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of nuclear weapons, we remain committed to advancing the treaties and humanitarian objectives and establishing an international trust fund for nuclear weapons victims. As co-chairs with Kazakhstan of the recent international meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation, we thank the Secretary-General for convening this important meeting and for keeping the needs of affected communities at the center of our collective efforts. Peace and security must also keep pace with emerging threats in the digital domain. The HIS Micronesian cable landed in Tarawa last year, connecting Kiribati with Nauru and the Federated States of Micronesia, transforming our connectivity and digital environment. However, it also creates vulnerabilities. With limited redundancy and technical capacity, island states face threats, including cybercrime, critical infrastructure attacks, and ransomware and online harms that can undermine security and development. Your Excellencies, Kiribati comes to this assembly not simply to speak of the challenges we face. We come here, we come to speak of the future we choose. Allow me to close, Mr. President, by bestowing upon the United Nations and all its members and all its staff our traditional blessings of the Maori, the Rai, or the Tabomo, meaning abundant wealth, peace, and prosperity. I thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President and Minister of Foreign Affairs and Immigration of the Republic of Kiribati. We shall now continue the general debate. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency, Hussain Mohamed Latheef, Vice President of the Republic of Maldives. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as President of the 81st Session. You can count on the full support of the Maldives as you lead this Assembly. I also thank former President of the General Assembly, High Excellency Aneleina Bebek, for her leadership of the 80th session. This year's theme, "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all", captures the task before us. Trust will not be restored by words alone. It will be restored by what this organization delivers for every country, large or small. 37 years ago, the Maldives asked this Assembly to face a simple truth. This small state can be highly vulnerable to external threats and acts of influence. In response, this Assembly adopted resolution 44/51, an initiative led by the Maldives, affirming the importance of protecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of small states. That was true then, and it is true even today. But the threats have evolved. Insecurity now travels through sea lanes, supply chains, financial markets, digital networks and new technologies. Today, sovereignty can be weakened without a single border being crossed. It can be undermined when external powers limit a state's freedom to choose. This is why the Maldives comes before this Assembly with a clear message: every state, large or small, must have the freedom and capacity to shape its own future. A sovereign future, and that future begins with peace. The Indian Ocean must remain peaceful. It must remain as a region where trade can flow and where states can prosper. Regional competition among major powers must not limit the choices of smaller states. Conflict does not have to reach our shores to affect us. In today's interconnected world, a crisis far away can quickly become a crisis at home. Interruption to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz raises fuel prices. It affects food supplies and air travel. The consequences of this are felt across tourism and public finances in the Maldives. The Maldives therefore condemns the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The strait must remain open and safe. The Maldives further condemns the attacks on Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Jordan. The Maldives appreciates the diplomatic efforts of Oman, Pakistan, and Qatar to de-escalate the crisis and bring the parties to dialogue. The right to a sovereign future must belong to all. And nowhere is that right more brutally denied than in Palestine. As genocide and war crimes against Palestinians continue, and their actions are not confined to Gaza. Its military attacks across the region have violated the sovereignty of other states. Security cannot be built by exporting insecurity. Nor can any country demand respect for its sovereignty while violating the sovereignty of others. No state should be shielded from accountability by its power or political alliances. But condemnation alone is not enough. Every member state must ask, what have we done to end this violence? The United Nations must ask itself the same question. The problem is not a lack of law. The rules are clear. What is absent is equal application. Humanitarians, international law cannot bind the weak and bend for the powerful. The same rules, the same standard, no exception. Israel's genocide in Gaza must end. Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine and other Arab lands must end. Illegal settlements must end. Humanitarian assistance must reach Palestinians safely, rapidly, and at scale. International courts and the resolution of this organization must be respected and implemented. For the Palestinian people, a sovereign future means freedom, dignity, self-determination, and the right to live their security in their own state. The Maldives will always stand with Palestinian people and their undeniable right for that future. This is why I reiterate our call for the recognition of independent and sovereign state of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital. And if this organization is restored trust and deliver for all, Palestine must become a full member of the United Nations. Conflict is not the only threat to sovereignty. Forces beyond our borders can also limit a state's freedom to shape its own future. For states like the Maldives, none is more consequential than climate change. For SIDS, climate change is altering the very physical foundations of our nations. Sea level rise is therefore not simply an environmental concern. It is a matter of national planning and national security. It is a matter of sovereignty. Let there be no doubt, rising seas may alter our shores, but they will not erase our statehood. They will not reduce our rights They will not weaken our maritime entitlements, and they will not diminish our national agency. Our response must be to adapt, innovate, and build. But resilience demands the means to act. That means finance must reach those who need it at the scale, at the speed, and on the terms needed to build resilience. This is why COP31 in Antalya must be a COP of delivery. Implementation must be the measure of commitment. We must move faster, we must speed up 2030 agenda, and we must turn our words into measurable progress for SIDS. For island nations, that progress cannot be separated from a healthy and sustainably managed ocean. Therefore, the first conference of the parties to the BBNJ Agreement must deliver from day one. Ultimately, global commitments matter only when they enable progress at home. His Excellency, President Dr. Mohamed Muiz, has set a clear ambition for the Maldives to become a developed country by 2040. We are pursuing that goal by raising productivity, diversifying our economy, building resilient infrastructure, expanding renewable energy, and investing in our people. Our future will be built by Maldivians. But the international system can widen or narrow our choices. Technology transfer, resilient supply chains, and accessible finance expand choice. Technological dependence, external shocks, and unsustainable debt limits it. This is why reform of the international financial architecture matters. We must implement the Cevier commitment and deliver on its promises on finance, debt, and reform. Earlier this year, the Mores joined other developing countries in launching the BRWAS platform. It must become a lasting mechanism that gives developing countries not just a place in the financial system, but a voice in shaping it. But for SEEDS, greater agency also depends on progress at home. We must build our institutions, improve stability, and attract responsible investment and meaningful partnerships. And these partnerships must build national capacity and support national ambitions. Partnerships must serve national needs, strengthen what we have, and leave us more capable than before. Our shared challenges can become our shared opportunities. This is the spirit of President Dr. Mohamed Muizz's Maldives First policy. Partnership built around respect national interest, and mutual contribution. And the same principle must guide the technological transformation before us. Artificial intelligence offers significant opportunities. For small states, AI can close distance. It can help overcome scale. And it can put better health care, education, and public services within reach. But these opportunities must be shared. Every country must have a voice in shaping the global rules for AI. The digital future should strengthen our ability to serve our people better, not create new forms of dependence. And as the world transforms, so must the United Nations. The UN80 initiative is an opportunity to reduce duplication, improve accountability, and focus resources on results. But efficiency must not be measured simply by what we cut. It must be measured by what we deliver. And the United Nations must not retreat from the countries that need it most in the name of efficiency. Reform must preserve a meaningful UN presence on the ground, particularly in seats. The UN development system must respond to the needs of program countries and remain guided by relevant international frameworks. The reform process must be member state-led. It must be inclusive and transparent. This is how reform will restore trust. by bringing the United Nations closer to the people in the countries it serves. Reform must also confront one of this organization's oldest weaknesses, unequal representation. The Security Council cannot reflect the world of 1945 while deciding for the world of today. It must be expanded in both permanent and non-permanent categories Seats must have a rotating seat. Africa must receive the representation long denied to it. And the veto must be abolished. After all, representation is not merely symbolic. Who sits at the table shapes what the table sees. Small states understand how closely climate, finance, trade, supply chains, and security are connected. We also know that international law is our strongest safeguard against unequal power. That principle must remain at the heart of the international system. The Maldives will take its seat on the Economic and Social Council for the 2027 to 2029 term. We are seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2028 to 2030 term. And we seek the support of member states for a seat on the UN Security Council for the 2033 to 2034 term. We do so. because small states must be decision makers, not decision takers. Representation matters not only within the bodies of this organization, but also in its leadership. As Secretary General Guterres approaches the end of a decade of service, the Maldives thank him for his leadership and commitment to international cooperation. The process to choose his successor must be transparent and based on merit. It must draw from the full breadth of talent available to this organization. For more than eight decades, every Secretary General has been a man. It is time for a woman to lead this organization. A leader who will defend the charter without exception, who can turn reform into delivery, and who will listen to all member states, including smallest. The task ahead is immense. The choice we make must meet it. So what should this assembly do? The Maudis proposes a simple test for a sovereign future. When we act on conflict, climate, finance, technology, or institutional reform, let us ask, Does this decision expand a status freedom tools? Does it build national capacity and reduce dependence? Does it protect sovereignty and independent decision making? If the answer is no, we must change course. And we must hold every state to the same standard. Let this be the measure of national international cooperation, not what we promise, but what we make possible. This is the measure of a United Nations that delivers for all. In 1989, the Maldives asked this Assembly to protect small states from external threats. Today, we ask it to protect something just as fundamental: every state's freedom to choose its own future. A future chosen by its people.

A future grounded in international law, a sovereign future for every state. I thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Vice President of the Republic of Maldives. The Assembly will now hear an address by His Excellency Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, Prime Minister of the Republic of Iraq. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

In the name of Allah, the most.

Gracious, the most merciful. Mr. President of the United Nations General Assembly, Your Excellency, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, Esteemed ladies and gentlemen, Peace be upon you and God's mercy and blessings. It is with great honor and pride that I stand before this international forum representing the Republic of Iraq, the home of the first civilizations, and where writing and law were born, and one of the founding members of the United Nations. I stand here to renew my country's commitment to the United Nations Charter and principles, and to present Iraq's vision for its future, its region, and the world at this critical juncture. Iraq, perhaps more than others, has experienced wars and the damage they cause. We have lived through the conditions they create, along with the siege and terrorism imposed on us. Our people have paid a hefty price and lost the lives of their children, their resources, and their development opportunities. Despite these difficulties that have made our country over several decades an arena of war and conflict, today, We are confidently presenting our vision for the future. Iraq aspires to exercise its influence and have an impact as an effective economic power in the region, and as a bridge for dialogue and cooperation among the peoples of the region. Ladies and gentlemen, our vision at this stage is based on our national will to restore the sanctity of the law, enhance state institutions, and strengthen citizens' trust in them. These are our governing priorities. We are striving to ensure that the state is the ultimate decision maker in matters of peace and war, and that weapons and tools of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions. This is so that the law is the final authority and national interest is the compass. Our implementation measures in this field are moving on track, as they represent the basis for building a state based on institutions, protecting sovereignty, ensuring stability, and creating the environment necessary for development and investment. With the end of the international coalition's mission in Iraq, we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners to a new phase, moving from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation in service of our common interests. In this manner, We add to Iraqis' victory over terrorism a redoubled determination and momentum to finish building our military and security capacities in order to protect our country, our people, and our sovereignty. In order to sustain integration with our international friends, we call on all partners to exercise border control, address gaps, and remain constantly vigilant in order to prevent the formation of an environment conducive to extremism. Ladies and gentlemen, in the context of institutional reform, our government is fighting a battle against corruption and for the protection of public funds. We are moving forward with sustainable core solutions in order to increase performance efficiency and improve providing services. We aim to build a strong state and a diversified and modern economy that keeps pace with global technological and digital transformations. And accordingly, We are working to employ all successful expertise and innovative experiences in the world of economics, finance, and business in service of a renaissance of economic and financial reform for my country. We also do this to provide a safe environment for national and foreign investment. This vision is based on the great potential Iraq possesses in terms of resources and investment opportunities in the fields of energy, industry, agriculture, transport, and technology, not to mention Iraq's exceptional geographical location, which connects its economy to the world. In this context, our vision aims to move Iraq to a stage where it can be an effective production partner in the region by gradually reducing the role of the rentier economy, strengthening open market policies, developing production and export capacities, and investing in infrastructure and services. On this basis, we have developed the appropriate roadmap to support the private sector, provide the necessary legal, tax, and customs facilities and guarantees for the growth of business and foreign trade, and build effective partnerships with the global market to accelerate achieving sustainable development. In the field of global energy, Iraq's influence is prominent as our government is adopting an ambitious program to increase the production of crude oil, in a manner consistent with the size of our proven reserves. Our government is also working to develop gas fields and expand refining capacities and our capacities to produce derivatives. And we are also working to improve our petrochemical industry capacities. Our ambition is for Iraq to be a global hub for energy production, and to leverage its potential to promote regional and international security and stability in a sustainable manner. Nevertheless, we express concern regarding developments concerned with freedom of transport and maritime navigation, and the crisis this has caused in terms of the rise of global energy prices. In order to contain the subsequent risks and the consequences on our peoples, we are working to diversify our oil export ports and develop energy lines and corridors linking Iraq, Turkey, Jordan, and Syria in order to reach global markets with the aim of contributing to energy security and diversifying supply routes. Excellencies, economic diversification on the basis of genuine partnerships is a central strategic objective of our economic policy. Therefore, our government has set among its priorities the goal of promoting economic and industrial development in all fields. The Development Road project comes as Iraq's comprehensive vision for regional complementarity, integration, and stability. It represents a vital gateway and a strategic corridor for trade, investment, industry, and energy, connecting the east with the west, starting from the Grand Al-Faw port to Turkey and from there on to Europe. We want for this project to be open to partnership with all our neighbors and friends, because we believe that economic interests create prosperity. When the countries of the region are connected, through ports, railways, power lines, trade and investments, they have a greater interest in preserving stability. Here, from the United Nations, we say to the world, invest with Iraq. Iraq has resources, markets, a good location, and the necessary will to build a new economy. Our government is hard at work to develop mutually beneficial partnerships, create employment opportunities, transfer technology and knowledge, and develop Iraq's productive capabilities. Ladies and gentlemen, the security of states and the maintenance of peace are a shared responsibility, as per the Charter of the United Nations. True stability is not built through wars, but through common interests that make cooperation more feasible than conflict. Iraq's vision is based on contributing to the region's transition from conflict to integration, from competition to cooperation, from resource depletion to investment in development. On this occasion, we extend our hands to everyone on the basis of respect for sovereignty, non-interference, good neighborliness, strengthening mutual interests, and adopting dialogue as a means to address differences. Based on these principles, Iraq renews its position in support of dialogue and diplomacy to defuse any crises. We also call for support for efforts for the passage of trade through Iraqi territory with great facilities in order to provide alternatives to complex trade corridors. Ladies and gentlemen, Iraq believes that our responsibility towards the peoples, their security and stability requires working to end conflicts through negotiation in order to secure a safe future and prevent future wars. Here at the United Nations Headquarters, there is a replica of the stele of the Babylonian King Hammurabi. It has an inscription which reads: Laws are made to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak. In today's world, we find the weak being oppressed because it is the law of the powerful that governs, not the power of the law. Therefore, the question of Palestine remains central to any discussion of stability in the region. There will be no room for security in the Middle East without a just solution for this issue and without establishing the right of the Palestinian people to their land, to self-determination, and to establishing their sovereign state. We stress here the paramount importance of facilitating humanitarian access and the protection of civilians. Ladies and gentlemen, the security we seek is not limited to halting conflicts, but rather includes confronting climate change, the effects of desertification and water scarcity. These are challenges that Iraq faces that affect its food security. Therefore, we affirm that we hold steadfastly onto our just and legitimate water rights, and we call for the joint management of water resources in accordance with the principles of cooperation and international law. In terms of risks, we continue to confront organized crime by cooperating with all friends to repel the dangers of organized crime and to abort the cross-border drug trade. We call for more information sharing and international coordination to ward off this danger that threatens societies. Amid these challenges, the well-being of the Iraqi people remains our ultimate objective and the focus of all of our efforts. Given the high proportion of young people in our society, we seek to make them a true driving force of the future economy through education, the diversification of employment opportunities, support for entrepreneurship, and the advancement of digital economy. At the same time, we remain committed, in accordance with the Constitution, to protecting human rights and freedoms, promoting women's participation, ensuring child welfare, and preserving the ethnic, religious, and cultural diversity of our country. Ladies and gentlemen, we confidently call upon you to engage more openly with Iraq, as it is a genuine partner capable of contributing to the promotion of security, the strengthening of stability, and the acceleration of development across all sectors. Today we say Iraq has never been on the margins. Rather, it is the heart of history beating in the modern world. Iraq is a nation worthy of partnership as we move toward the future. In conclusion, we reaffirm our support for the United Nations' role and express our appreciation for its efforts, which have embodied collective action in support of Iraq through the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI. And we underscore our commitment to fostering productive cooperation with the organization and wish it success in its endeavors to mitigate the effects of wars and the consequences of conflict around the world. May God's peace, mercy, and blessings be upon you all.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Republic of Iraq. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Nawaf Salam, President of the Council of Ministers of the Lebanese Republic. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General, The more I reflect on the theme of this session of the General Assembly, "Restoring trust and managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all," the more convinced I become of the wisdom of that choice. Without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among States. nor can cooperation among them flourish. More than 80 years ago, the United Nations was founded on the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force. Yet, we still live in a world of multiplying wars and conflicts, a world that spends more on armaments than on development. Civilians remain the primary victims. while millions face displacement, hunger, and deprivation. The problem is not the absence of rules. It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application. The sovereignty of states cannot be untouchable in one place and negotiable in another, nor can the rules of international law apply to some but not to others. Restoring trust requires respect for international law. It requires investment in preventing conflicts before they erupt and in development before poverty and deprivation become a source of violence, extremism, and terrorism. Development, too, is a matter of peace. There can be no sustainable peace in a world of widening economic disparities. where some states spend more on servicing their debt than on the health of their citizens and the education of their children. This does not absolve developing countries of the responsibility to undertake reform, combat corruption and build institutions. But those efforts require a fairer and more equitable international economic order, one that offers them genuine opportunities to advance. Mr. President, our shared responsibility is equally evident in the face of the profound transformations our world is undergoing. Climate change threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions. Those countries that have contributed least to it bear its gravest consequences. This calls for equitable adaptation, finance, and technology transfer. At the same time, the artificial intelligence revolution is opening unprecedented horizons for progress across every sphere of life. Yet it also raises challenges for the future of work and for human rights and fundamental freedoms. This calls for international governance that places the human being with his or her freedom and privacy at the heart of this transformation. Above all, we must not allow an artificial intelligence divide to emerge on top of the existing gaps in wealth and development. Restoring trust requires that every individual feel that the law protects them, that development do not exclude them, and that progress leaves no one behind. Mr. President, if restoring trust is a challenge facing our world today, for Lebanon, it is not a mere slogan. Just as managing transformation is not an option up for debate. Together, they constitute the very essence of the mission we pledged before our people, before our Arab brothers, and before the entire world on the day I was entrusted with leading the government of Lebanon. We assumed this responsibility at a time when our country faced three existential challenges. The first was to regain the trust of its people after the financial collapse and the Beirut port explosion and the tragedies and wounds they left behind. The second was to reclaim its national decision-making, so that no authority stands above that of the state, no weapons exist outside its armed forces, and no decision on war and peace is taken outside its constitutional institutions. The third was to recover all of its territory from Israeli occupation and to extend its sovereignty over the entirety of its national soil through its own forces in implementation of the Taif Agreement and in sincere respect for the relevant international resolutions on Lebanon. Foremost among these is Resolution 1701, which remains to this day a fundamental point of reference governing relations between Lebanon and Israel. Trust rebuilt, decision-making reclaimed, land liberated, that is the equation for Lebanon's recovery. These are not three separate challenges. They are three facets of a single cause. Restoring a state that its citizens trust, that is master of its own decisions, and that exercises sovereignty over the whole of its territory. Mr. President, First, the trust we seek to restore is not trust in words. It is trust in institutions that protect rights, in a judiciary that guarantees justice, in an economy that restores prosperity to the people and gives young people the opportunity of a better future. We cannot speak of restoring trust without recalling the Beirut port explosion. The wound of the 4th of August remains open. It cannot heal without truth, justice, and accountability. And these will inevitably come. Some may feel that our government has not yet fulfilled all of its commitments. We do not claim that the task is complete. But fairness, demands that we not overlook the scale of legacy we inherited: paralyzed institutions, a public administration of diminished effectiveness, an economy stripped of the foundations of growth, and a state weakened by compounding crises and by decades of external interference. Even though, we have not used the difficulty of our circumstances as a pretext to retreat from our commitments. and we will not retreat. Lebanon has launched reforms on several fronts. namely revitalizing the public administration, strengthening the independence of the judiciary, modernizing the media law, and abolishing the death penalty. It is also advancing towards the completion of financial reforms aimed at restoring order to the financial system and recovering depositors' funds. These reforms should pave the way for an agreement with the IMF. Such an agreement is an indispensable tool for restoring international confidence in Lebanon and a gateway to securing the financing needed from all our regional and international partners for economic recovery and reconstruction. Our aim in pursuing reform is not to ask our people to renew their trust in the state. Rather, through reform, we seek to rebuild a state worthy of its people's trust. Second, a state does not regain the trust of its citizens through reform alone, but also by reclaiming its national decision-making. In that spirit, we did not merely affirm the principle that weapons must be exclusively in the hands of the state and that decisions on war and peace rest solely with its constitutional institutions. We translated that commitment into decisions taken by the Council of Ministers, notably in August and September of last year and again in March of this year. That was after Lebanon found itself in a war that it did not choose. It was imposed upon us despite our repeated warnings of the dangers of being drawn into it. As the war in the region widened and initiatives to end it multiplied, we held fast to a non-negotiable principle: no one speaks for Lebanon, and no one negotiates on its behalf, except the Lebanese state through its constitutional institutions. It is true that Lebanon is affected by developments in its surroundings. It is true that Lebanon is affected by developments in its surroundings. That does not mean, however, that we accept its becoming, once again, an arena for the conflicts of others or a bargaining chip in their hands. Lebanon's future will not be decided on its behalf nor may its security and stability become the price of settlements concluded in its absence third our position on the war has been clear from the outset we want it to end we want the ceasefire consolidated we want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders in accordance with the 1990 with the 1949 General Armistice agreement and as firm by resolution 1701 we want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and the reconstruction of what the war has destroyed. It was in that spirit that the Lebanese state entered into negotiations with Israel under the kind auspices of the United States of America and its president, for which we are grateful. with a view to reaching arrangements that ensure an end to the war and the restoration of Lebanon's full sovereignty. The sovereignty to which we are committed is indivisible. It requires Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory. It equally requires the extension of the authority of the Lebanese state through its own forces over the entirety of its territory, with weapons held by the state alone. It is on these two principles and on the basis of reciprocity and phased implementation that the tripartite framework reached in the negotiations rests. However, the success of any agreement is measured not by declared intentions, but by fulfillment of commitments. What is required today, therefore, is to complete the translation of this framework into practical steps. within a clear timetable and with a verification mechanism that ensures the implementation of all its provisions. Mr. President, in this context, I must pay tribute to the role played by the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon and to the courage of its leadership, personnel and staff, and their sacrifices in preserving stability, supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces, and implementing Resolution 1701. To all the countries that have contributed troops to this force, Lebanon extends its profound thanks and appreciation. We have taken note of Security Council Resolution 2790 of 2025. 2025, which decided to terminate UNIFIL's operations at the end of this year and to begin its gradual withdrawal, and requested the Secretary-General to explore available options for the continued implementation of resolution 1701. What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it. Such a force should ensure the continuation of monitoring, reporting and liaison functions, and its role should complement the requirements for implementing the tripartite framework. Mr. President, recovering the Mr. President, recovering the land does not mean only the withdrawal of occupying forces. It also means the return of its inhabitants and the revival of life in their villages and towns. The war has left behind a vast humanitarian crisis in Lebanon. It has caused extensive destruction to housing, public facilities, infrastructure, and productive sectors, and has deprived large numbers of Lebanese of their homes and livelihoods. While we thank the United Nations entities and our international partners for their humanitarian contributions, we call at the same time for continued funding to meet the basic needs of those affected, particularly the displaced, in parallel with the requirements of early recovery, as well as reconstruction and development. The reconstruction of the South is not merely the rebuilding of stone; it is the rebuilding of people's lives, the restoration of their livelihoods, and the affirmation of their right to live in safety and dignity on their land. Mr. President, the Lebanon that stands before you today does not shirk its responsibilities, nor does it ask others to do what It is duty-bound to do itself. We are shouldering our responsibility for reform and for extending the authority of the state over the entirety of our territory. But we are entitled to ask the international community to shoulder, in turn, its responsibility to ensure respect for Lebanon's sovereignty and the implementation of resolutions of international legitimacy. Mr. President. There can be no lasting stability in Lebanon without lasting stability in our region. And there can be no stability in the region as long as this organization remains unable to enable the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination, like all other peoples of the world, no less and no more. This is despite the dozens of resolutions adopted by this Assembly and by the Security Council that lay clear foundations for that right, not to mention the Arab Peace Initiative. As for the tragedy of wounded Gaza, it has put the conscience of the world and the inability of its institutions to a test from which there can be no escape. I must stress here that cutting off funding to UNRWA or undermining its mandate does not end the rights of Palestinian refugees. even if that's what some seek. On the contrary, it compounds their suffering, jeopardizes the prospects for a just and lasting solution to their cause, and increases the burden on host countries, foremost among them Lebanon. With regard to the security situation in the region, Lebanon wishes to renew its solidarity with the states of the Arab Gulf and with Jordan in the face of Iranian attacks that threaten regional security and the freedom and safety of maritime navigation. The effects of these attacks are not confined to theaters of confrontation. They extend to supply chains, to the prices of goods, particularly food and energy, and to inflation rates. Mr. President, allow me to conclude by returning once more to the theme of this session of the General Assembly: restoring trust. and managing transformation for a United Nations that delivers for all. The truth is that we cannot call on the states of the world to change their conduct while failing to make the necessary changes within our own organization so that it delivers the results expected of it and regains the trust of the peoples of the world. The reality is that the world has changed profoundly since 1945. The membership of the United Nations has grown nearly fourfold. Colonialism has ended. Africa has risen. Asia has been transformed, and new powers have emerged. The balance of the global economy has shifted. Yet, the basic composition of the Security Council remains captive to a historical moment dating back to the end of the Second World War. Africa and the Arab world cannot remain without permanent representation on the Council, nor can small and medium-sized states remain mere spectators to decisions that concern their security and their future. We know that Security Council reform is a complex matter, but the difficulty of reform is no argument against its necessity. Indeed, reform of the United Nations must begin here, with the Security Council. For it is the Security Council that bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Therefore, once again, add Lebanon's voice to that of the majority of the members of our organization in calling for an expansion of the Security Council that achieves more inclusive and equitable representation. Being realists, we do not call for the abolition of the veto. Rather, we call for restraint in its use in cases of genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and serious violations of international humanitarian law. We insist on reform of the United Nations only because we want it to be a more representative, more democratic, and more effective organization. We want an organization true to the purposes and principles of its charter, yet ever renewed, so that it may rise to the challenges of our rapidly changing world and meet the aspirations of our peoples and their new generations. I thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Council of Ministers of the Lebanese Republic. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Christophe Mermoud, Minister of State, Head of Government of the Principality of Monaco. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, Heads of State, Heads of Government, Delegates, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am addressing you as the representative of the smallest Member State of this Organization in terms of its land mass and one of the smallest in terms of its population, barely two squared kilometers bordering the Mediterranean. And yet, in this forum, there are no small or large states. Here, every one of the 193 members has a voice, one alone, and of the same weight. Here, the Charter only recognizes states equal in sovereignty, equal in rights, but also, and I wish to stress this point, equal in terms of responsibility. Because the equality that our organization bestows upon us is not a privilege that we enjoy, it is a responsibility that we bear. This responsibility is our shared, unique duty to uphold the law and multilateralism. Shared because no state, regardless of how powerful it is, can preserve peace alone or address global threats alone. unique because everybody must shoulder it without leaving it to others to honor the promise of San Francisco. It is this message that His Serene Highness Prince Albert II, the Prince of Monaco, charged me with bringing to this rostrum with his greetings of trust and friendship. President, the Principality of Monaco wishes sincerely to congratulate you upon your election to the presidency of this 81st session, for which you have chosen the topic, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a UN that Delivers for All. You can count on the full support of my country. And I also wish to warmly thank the Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, who is finishing his second mandate amidst particularly grave circumstances. Why does a state such as mine believe so strongly in international law? The answer goes for all. When might makes right, it is the smallest states who are the first to be threatened. When force is regulated by the law, all of humanity is protected. Sovereign equality between states, honouring commitments, peacefully settling disputes are therefore not abstract concepts. They are our front line of protection, and yours too, with the balance, as is set out by the Charter, between the three pillars: peace and security, development, and human rights. Nevertheless, this protection is today under assault. Rearmament is accelerating throughout the world. We are seeing The use of force, once again, as being another political tool for some, trade is breaking down, and we're seeing a race to capture critical resources. The private sector is also part of these power relations. We are now in the era of the geo-economy, and this is fertile ground for disinformation, which undermines people's trust in their institutions and leads them to question verifiable facts. Our belief has never been tried to such an extent since 1945. In Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, the Sahel, in many other places out of the media spotlight, civilians are paying the price for conflicts which have discarded the most basic rules of humanity. And never since 1945 has the very legitimacy of states and multilateral bodies such as the UN been called into question to such an extent. Given this danger, let us recall our mission in the words of Dag Hammarskjold, the second Secretary-General of the UN. The UN was not created to take mankind to heaven, but to save humanity from hell. That is the exact scope of our task, and that is why we do not have the right to give up. First, in Ukraine. For almost five years, a permanent member of the Security Council has been waging a war of aggression against a sovereign state, in flagrant violation of the Charter. From the very outset, Monaco condemned this aggression, unambiguously and unreservedly. We voted in favour of all of the General Assembly's resolutions calling and demanding for Russian forces to withdraw. We took all restrictive measures aligned with EU measures. And we also provided our humanitarian support to the Ukrainian people and hosted people displaced by the war. Our support is unwavering and it will remain so. Monaco will never recognize any annexation of territory obtained through force. Allowing this for one state would be tantamount to allowing it for all. The Principality welcomes the ongoing diplomatic efforts and hopes that they will lead to fair, comprehensive, lasting peace, respecting Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Next to the Middle East, Monaco was greatly relieved by the ceasefire which entered into force in Gaza and the fact that the hostages were freed. Nothing can ever justify the acts of terror of the 7th of October, but nor can anything justify the price paid by the civilians in Gaza. The Principality calls on all parties to strengthen the fragile ceasefire and to respect every stage of it, ensuring full, safe, unhindered humanitarian access. We support efforts to rebuild Gaza, and we are concerned about the ongoing violence in the West Bank, in the occupied territories, which ride roughshod over human rights and dishonour democratic values. Our belief remains the same. The only viable option is the two-state solution, Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace and security. within safe and recognized borders. Any policy that makes that scenario less likely, through settlement building or sowing terror, makes peace less likely too. In Lebanon too, Monaco supports de-escalation efforts and calls on all parties to fulfill their commitments, first and foremost Security Council Resolution 1701. The people of Lebanon have the right to a fully sovereign state in peace throughout its territory. In the Persian Gulf, finally, tensions around Iran remain a source of deep concern. Monaco pays tribute to all the civilian victims of the conflict and reiterates its solidarity with the countries of the Gulf who have been affected by the attacks. Here again, only negotiations can lead to a global agreement on the Iranian nuclear program and will prevent further escalation. Above and beyond these crises, Monaco will continue to contribute to international cooperation, focused on the least developed countries, through its support to the International Committee for the Red Cross, the High Commissioner for Refugees, and the World Food Program. through development aid geared towards the health, education and empowerment of women and girls. Restoring trust also means changing the organization itself. Monaco supports the UN80 initiative to make the organization more streamlined, more understandable, more efficient and closer to people on the ground. Still, the UN needs resources to function. My country fulfills its financial contributions in full and on time, and we call on all other states to do likewise. But this necessary step is not enough in the light of the changes that have to be undertaken. That is why Monaco calls on the real leaders of the United Nations to rethink the architecture of our system. from 2030, bringing on board the public and private sector, civil society, and educational and cultural hubs. Streamlining processes, preventing mandate duplication, consolidating specialized agencies, regional centers, and the secretariat, and guaranteeing small states genuine inclusivity. There is plenty of work to do. The time of the law is patient, But this patience should not be confused with inertia. In the same vein, the Principality is in favour of a reform of the Security Council to make it more representative to today's realities, while also preserving its ability to act. And we're also in favour of the revitalization of this General Assembly, the house of equality between states. This session will also see the election of the next Secretary General of the organization. Monaco calls for a transparent, inclusive, and rigorous process. After 80 years, the principality hopes that women candidates will be seriously considered. The organization would do well to demonstrate at its helm the equality for which it stands. Ladies and gentlemen, there is one area where multilateral trust has recently produced tangible results, and it is dear to the heart of His Serene Highness Prince Albert II, and that is to say, the ocean. The entry into force of the Agreement on Marine Biodiversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, which Monaco was one of the first countries to sign and ratify, is a victory of the law over seizure, of cooperation over predation. We now need to translate these commitments into acts to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030, to finally agree on an ambitious and binding agreement on plastics pollution, and exercise extreme caution with regards to deep seabed mining. The ocean is nobody's property. It is everyone's responsibility. Monaco will continue to do its part in this vital task, relying on science, which is the only universal compass. And what goes for the ocean also goes for the climate. The Paris Agreement remains our common framework. Monaco will honor its commitments by reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 67.5% by 2030 and by achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The Principality calls on all countries to show more ambition in their national contributions and not to abandon island and coastal states, which are the most vulnerable. Because the climate crisis is no longer a distant threat, heat waves, fires and floods are multiplying, and the Mediterranean, which my country borders, experienced last year its second highest surface temperature ever recorded. And because science is being questioned, let us recall, as the Prince did in COP30 in Belem, that science has never been as certain, as accessible and as clear. Four years before the 2030 deadline, the Sustainable Development Agenda must not become the symbol of our broken promises. Let us be candid as we take stock. States alone cannot make progress. We need to have a renewed framework for cooperation with those who create wealth and shape innovation, businesses first and foremost, and civil society. Lastly, preparing for the future and ensuring it benefits everyone means mastering technological changes. Artificial intelligence is creating enormous opportunities for human development, But it also entails genuine risks. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance, which was held this year in Geneva, confirmed this. These technologies must remain at the service of humanity, and the United Nations cannot remain a spectator. Monaco supports the implementation of the Global Digital Compact and a new normative framework on AI. based on law and shared ethical principles, respecting human rights and being accessible to all states. Finally, the Principality calls for strengthened cooperation to deal with cyber threats and for inclusive transitions, both within states and within societies. President, When he received the Nobel Prize in Literature, the great French writer Albert Camus defined the task of his generation thus: not to reform the world, but perhaps even greater, to prevent the world from destroying itself. Today, that is our task, preventing the world from destroying itself, preventing law being destroyed by force, preventing trust being destroyed by mistrust, and preventing the planet from being destroyed under the weight of our negligence. Trust is not decreed, it is won, through deeds and through promises kept. That is the overarching principle that a state such as mine aims to fulfil, being consistent, keeping our word. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of His Serene Highness Prince Albert II, I wish to reiterate the commitment of Monaco to the United Nations, to its Charter, and to the ideal that led to its establishment, saving future generations from the scourge of war, and building together a common house where even the smallest states can take their rightful place, because here the law protects them all. This pledge will only be fulfilled through the might of the law and not through might makes right. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Minister of State, Head of Government of the Principality of Monaco. The Assembly will hear an address by Her Excellency Hilda Heine, President of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. I request protocol to escort Her Excellency and invite her to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, I ask every nation here, are we still willing to work together? The principles in the UN Charter affirmed by each one of us taking our seat in this hall, are now tested not by argument, but by neglect or ill intention. The credibility and effectiveness of multilateral institutions is imperative for small nations. It is past time to better turn the urgency expressed in political declarations and resolutions into results not repetition. We speak from our own experience when we underscore the importance of acting together. An institution that takes decisions collectively must also be accountable collectively. Mr. President, the United Nations is long overdue to reflect and renew the same spirit with which our Marshallese people first came to the United Nation by delivering an apology and acknowledgement of the harm caused by impacts from the 67 nuclear weapons tested on our islands during our time as a UN strategic trust territory between 1946 and 1958. The sacred trust of the UN trusteeship to ensure our well-being was jeopardized by these tests, and the lack of full acknowledgment remains a moral failing. For generations, our families have testified to displacement, illness, contamination, and loss, all of them impacts to our core human rights. As our survivors would say, and I quote, "This is a song that has been sung far too many times," unquote. It was in the same building that the UN Trusteeship Council sat in session and voted on Resolutions 1082 and 1493 in 1954 and 1956, respectively, to effectively authorize further nuclear testing over the demands of our local leaders and many citizens. The United Nations ultimately allowed the testing to continue, but the shock and tragedy of nuclear exposure in the Marshall Islands was a profound driver of the 1963 global ban on atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons. We acknowledge the ongoing actions, dialogues, and complex legacy of the UN's administering authority, the United States, but the role of the United Nations cannot pass without comment. For us and for fellow member states, this apology is an opportunity to reflect upon the past, to bring healing and closure to the Marshallese people. We carry no larger agenda other than to ensure that the United Nations will do better. Mr. President, as we face a world in which scientists tell us overshooting the 1.5 degree temperature limit that we agreed in Paris is increasingly likely, we all need to wake up and act. Our focus now must be on preventing or minimizing the overshoot. shortening the time we spend above 1.5, and doing everything possible to fight our way back. As we gather in Tuvalu, Fiji, and Turkey for this year's climate pre-COP and COP, our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming. A much accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is the only logical response. Continued investment in fossil fuels is not only immoral, but irrational. Technologies exist which provide secure, stable, zero-emissions energy. We are employing them in my own country, where in the next 18 months, renewable energy will cut fossil fuel use in our remote outer islands by 88 percent. giving many access to electricity for the first time. We must do everything in our power to accelerate the deployment of renewables and to reduce fossil fuel production and consumption with equal speed. This includes shipping, where we have the opportunity at the International Maritime Organization to adopt binding regulations that will place international shipping on a clear path to net zero by 2050 and generate the revenue required to ensure a just and equitable transition. Mr. President, the denials and delays that have slowed the transition away from fossil fuels mean that countries like mine are already experiencing grave challenges. We have developed our national adaptation plan, working across ministries and with our people to determine how to make a safe future. Adapting is costly and takes time, even as we've seen schools destroyed by rising seas, saltwater poisoning our wells, and disease outbreaks linked to environmental change. This injustice must be addressed. Our communities deserve restitution. The Marshall Islands and vulnerable people everywhere need sufficient, timely, and accessible finance for adaptation and loss and damage. Those who have profited to the detriment of the many must pay. We have created homegrown institutions that are ready and willing to respond. like the Pacific Resilience Facility, a regionally managed platform, and the Marshall Islands Adaptation and Resilience Trust Fund, designed to enable donors to support our adaptation efforts. Mr. President, the crisis has the power to divide us or to prove that we all remain willing to achieve common goals. This week, the Marshall Islands convened the High Ambition Coalition, a diverse group of countries committed to a rigorous response to the climate crisis. We are united in the view that the best available science must lead the decisions we make. The importance of a 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature limit, an urgent transition away from fossil fuels, and the need for adequate and accessible climate finance, especially for adaptation and loss and damage. Mr. President, as a low-lying atoll nation with no higher ground, sea level rise is an immediate and stark reality. This week's UN high-level meeting on sea level rise has helped achieve new understanding in international law. It is the seas that are rising around us, and not our islands which are sinking. Our boundaries and baselines of today, the political footprint on the map, will endure in the face of aggressive sea level rise scenarios. Our collective stability and security as Pacific Islands Forum members and as a UN member state will be now better addressed. As an atoll nation, our tide gauge is proof enough that far more action is needed. And we are acting. Confronted with rising seas on our most vulnerable shorelines, we completed the Yibai seawall and footpath last week, 1.8 kilometers of ocean-side protection, built with support from the World Bank, the Green Climate Fund, and our own resources. Engineered by rising seas, it now protects 8,400 people and critical energy infrastructure, reduces annual coastal flooding losses, and anchors resilient future development on Ebeye, including schools, housing, and the proposed new hospital, while providing a safe public space that strengthens community well-being. It cost $75 million, took 70,000 tons of rocks, took more than a decade to do, and it is just one island of over 1,000. We are taking action, and we urgently need strengthened partnership to better protect our islands before sea level rise overtakes us. Mr. President, my nation underscores the importance of the Law of the Sea as a key legal pillar of our future. Even before we were a UN member, we fought closely both to participate in UN Law of the Sea negotiations and to secure these rights in our constitution. Pacific Island leadership and that of all small island developing states as we find every multilateral milestone for oceans and fisheries, and we will continue to do so. As an ocean people, the consequences of getting it wrong are not from distant impacts, but adjacent to our waters, particularly in the North Pacific, both within the International Seabed Authority and unilateral actions. Collectively, the people and voices of Micronesia must be heard. We are joined by Guam, Northern Marianas, Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau in expressing our alarm at seabed mining actions where the decisions are made before impacts are well understood and where adequate safeguards remain undefined. The Marshall Islands joined 45 nations seeking a moratorium on seabed mining. Responsible and science-driven regulations need to be in place. Going on guesswork for global oceans is beyond dangerous. There are no do-overs. The Marshall Islands look forward to the first Conference of Parties to the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction. to work across silos to advance ICS protection. We urge wide ratification of the agreement. The Marshall Islands look forward to supporting its secretariat in a host nation committed to upholding the law of the sea as a matter of both principle and law, in words and in actions. Mr. President, too often the word geopolitics is considered to refer only to the whims of superpowers and not the reality of our fragile place between them. As a region of vulnerable island nations, we rightly define our own security priorities, and these deeply cut across every sector, placing a safe future for our youngest generation beyond grasp. As fuel and energy costs are rising beyond our ability to respond, impacts from bigger power plays halfway around the world are amplified tenfold in small, remote economies. The international community is not listening closely to small island developing states, and it is not responding fast enough. Too often, the purported solutions for island nations don't seem to know the problem. Mr. President, the Marshall Islands faces complex challenges in tackling the SDGs, but we committed with all of our efforts to ensure no one is left behind. Our national planning is now firmly linked to SDG goals and targets, and our actions proves our commitment. We have developed direct assistance to vulnerable groups, including mothers and early childhood development, and we are also reaching out to our entire in-country population with quarterly supplemental income and improved access to digital finance tools. Our aspirations must be better matched by partnership and island-scale investment and policy innovation. I must underscore the direct need for data capacity support to measure progress and effectiveness for small island developing states. If we cannot assess the SDGs, we cannot correct course. Mr. President, The Marshall Islands affirms the region Pacific Islands Forum communicate position regarding West Papua, including the 2018 invitation by Indonesia to the UN Human Rights Commissioner. Further, the Marshall Islands strongly welcomes recent calls for a ministerial summit between ASEAN and the Pacific Islands Forum to take forward our 2023 agreement. our two regions can stand united as neighbors and close friends. The Marshall Islands affirms its longstanding support for Japan and its G4 partners to achieve permanent membership on the UN Security Council. Mr. President, the Marshall Islands expresses its grave concern over increased efforts to spread dangerous disinformation in these halls. Taiwan and its 23 million people are an objective reality, and only its democratically elected government can represent it. Appropriate ways must be found for Taiwan's substantive participation in UN meetings if the UN is to be truly inclusive and effective. In years to come, every nation in this hall may be told that the question or coercion upon Taiwan is an internal matter, somehow justified by an ancient UN Seeding Chart resolution, a resolution which doesn't even reference Taiwan. In years to come, we may all be told that it's futile for small nations to resist a larger one. and that might makes right, regardless of the rulebook. We all will experience pressure to accept a false narrative that UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 somehow serves as a legal pretext under the UN Charter for coercion or war, impairing freedom of navigation in one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. We will be asked politely and impolitely to turn a blind eye and look away. It is vital that every nation here, including our close partners in our own region, know that a peace man never satisfies an aggressor's wider agenda. And one taste is never enough. How the UN addresses this very real security dilemma will be a test of its strength and relevance. Excellencies, the Marshall Islands stands firm in investing ourselves in this multilateral institution with clear sight of its frustrations and grave errors. Two years ago, I concluded my statement by reciting an old Marshallese proverb, "Wetin kangal, wetin kangal." It describes the coral reef where different species of fish congregate to feed and seek shelter. Today, we are not only being called upon to revitalize this 81-year-old institution created from the ashes of global conflict, but we are being challenged to address the complexities of a rapidly changing world. The United Nations must continue to serve as our primary to ensure that no one is left behind. Thank you, commoltava.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of the Marshall Islands. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Robert Abela, Prime Minister of the Republic of Malta. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Dear Friends, The chosen theme for this year's General Assembly is "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation". I don't think that there could be a more appropriate framing for our discussions of this week. Trust. or more properly, the lack thereof, is the greatest challenge currently facing our world. The erosion of trust that has gripped our societies runs deep. Where once people embraced trust, now people are gripped by suspicion. Suspicion of governments, suspicion of institutions, suspicion of businesses, even, all too often, suspicion of each other. I am talking about suspicion, not skepticism. Skepticism, the legitimate questioning of those who hold power over people's lives, is the lifeblood of a democratic society. Suspicion, however, the assumption that others are automatically looking out for their interests and not those of the common good, is poison to any democratic society. No community can succeed if we blindly believe that our neighbors are out to do us down, just as no country can succeed if it blindly believes that its neighbors, even those it may long have considered and seen as friends, are out to get it. Which means restoring trust, rebuilding alliances, remaking friendships must be the central mission for all of us here, at home and abroad. It must also be the central mission of the remaking of this United Nations. To change, you have to believe. We know we need to change how the United Nations works, how it takes decisions, and how it delivers on the ground. But we can only make that change, achieve that transformation, if we believe that change is possible. Nobody ever successfully renovated a house without the faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result would be a real improvement on what went before. So, we need to show faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way the end result of transforming this House this home of all the nations, will be a real step forward. And as this United Nations embarks on its ninth decade of service, the need for a step change in how the international community works together, solves problems together, is arguably needed more acutely now than ever before. That erosion of trust is leading to the corrosion of the international order, not the improvement of the international order, but the destruction of the international order. An international order that, for all its flaws and failures, has seen more children escape hunger, more families live in peace, and more children grow into old age than any era before it. To destroy the international settlement without any idea of what comes next would be an act of wanton destruction that would rightly never be forgiven or forgotten by the tens of millions whose future it would betray. So, let us be bold and let us say it loud and clear. Let us be utterly unequivocal Now, more than ever, is a moment for more cooperation, not less, more dialogue, not less, more trust, not less. That is the only way that we will manage to find paths to progress on the all too many, all too intractable conflicts blighting our world today. In Malta, the smallest member state of the European Union. We have always been a bridge between Europe and the Middle East. So, allow me to focus on two of those conflicts on our doorstep. Firstly, Ukraine. It is all too easy and all too great a mistake for us to fall in the trap that repelling the invasion of Ukraine becomes Another never-ending conflict. A grinding tragedy on the corner of our continent about which we can do nothing. Malta will never accept that despair. Europe must never accept that despair. The world must never turn its head away in despair. Malta remains a sediment in our condemnation of that invasion today as we were on day one in February 2022. And Malta is equally as adamant that a just and lasting peace must guarantee Ukraine's sovereignty within its internationally recognized borders. That will only come about through a diplomatic process that the Ukrainian people can have full trust in. They will only have such trust if the process follows a full and unconditional ceasefire and the full participation of Ukraine and its people in the subsequent peace talks. Rightly, the Ukrainian people will never have trust in any such for a settlement which involves their government being frogmarched to the table, one arm tied behind its back, whilst the guns still blaze. The issue of trust is clearly also central to the very worrying situation in Gaza. The people of Israel need to have trust that Hamas will be disarmed and that they will play no future role in the governance or security structures of Gaza.
