Trust in the international system begins with the conviction that everyone matters, and that the security of small states is as precious as that of great powers. International conflicts far from our shores in Ukraine and the Middle East continue to have devastating consequences for our daily lives, disrupting agricultural trade and global food stability, and driving up fuel prices and shipping premiums. We therefore join others here and call for an immediate end to the war in Ukraine, with full respect for state sovereignty and territorial integrity under the UN Charter. And likewise, we call for a permanent ceasefire in the Middle East, the protection of civilians, and the realization of a two-state solution guaranteeing peace and security for Palestine and Israel. Mr. President, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines does not stand alone. We stand with our brothers and sisters in the Caribbean community, CARICOM. Which is not just a trading block, but a family whose members in these uncertain times, need each other more than ever. For us in the Caribbean, peace and security are paramount concerns in our diplomatic efforts. Therefore, as we seek to restore trust, we reaffirm that Latin America and the Caribbean must remain a zone of peace, where disputes are settled through peaceful means, with adherence to international law and the UN Charter. We urge that the territorial dispute between Venezuela and Guyana be resolved in this manner. Within our hemisphere, Other unresolved challenges require immediate principled engagement. Haiti remains our urgent concern. Nearly four decades ago, the Trinidadian calypsonian David Rudder sang a lament to Haiti. His words are still relevant today. I quote, "When there is anguish in Port-au-Prince, it's still Africa crying." We are outing fires in far away places when our neighbors are burning. I refuse to believe that we good people will forever turn our hearts and our eyes away. Haiti, I am sorry. And the song goes on. The insecurity of the Haitian people, plagued by gang violence and political uncertainty, is a pain felt across our region. We support the efforts of Caricom and this organization to help fund and provide security to build up critical institutions and create a viable path to general elections. We must confront the reality of arms trafficking including assault weapons that are terrorizing Haitian communities and indeed communities across the Caribbean. We don't make these weapons in the Caribbean. They are manufactured in industrial nations and smuggled across borders into our region, into our countries. We therefore call upon all countries to take decisive action to stem the illicit flow of weapons and ammunitions across borders and into the Caribbean. Mister President, Cuba has long been a valued member of our Caribbean family. For more than three decades, this Assembly has said that the economic embargo imposed on Cuba must end. Whatever disagreements exist, the collective punishment of an entire population, denying medicine, denying trade, denying fuel, denying ordinary development, cannot be reconciled with the Charter we all signed. My Government adds its voice to call a call renewed year after year in this hall for the embargo to end. When earthquake, devastating earthquake struck Venezuela earlier this year, claiming thousands of lives. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines stood up in solidarity. Contributing emergency assistance through a coordinated CARICOM relief effort. Mister President, When tragedy strikes, we must act as our brothers' and sisters' keepers. This, too, builds and restores trust among nations and strengthens the United Nations. Mr. President, friendship also forms -- is a form of trust, and I wish in this august body to recognize our country's 45 years of diplomatic ties and friendship with Taiwan that has seen us work together in development, in disaster response, education, and in public health. Taiwan has shown time and again that they are prepared to be a responsible member of the international community. We renew our call for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the United Nations system and its specialized agencies. Mister President, let us also restore trust through support for reparatory justice. The past is not the past. When its consequences still shape who is rich and who is poor in the world today. The Caribbean community has for over a decade advanced a ten-point plan for reparatory justice, seeking acknowledgement, repair, and genuine partnership to address the historic injustices of the enslavement of African people and the near annihilation of our indigenous populations. We are encouraged that in March 2026, this Assembly strongly adopted a resolution sponsored by Ghana and supported by the African Union and CARICOM, declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. This is a hopeful and historic event. And after the follow-up conference in Accra in June, momentum grows, so necessary actions must follow. When the continent from which our enslaved ancestors were taken and the islands to which they were brought in change, in chains, spoke in one voice, this chamber listened. The world listened. We expect that more steps will follow. From discussions that will be held as part of the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda in November. As I conclude, Mr. President, we ask how the United Nations can restore trust while managing transformation. In summary, trust is restored when the smallest and most vulnerable nations feel they are included and that their concerns are addressed. Trust is restored when a national debt is restructured to be fairer. It is restored when hurricane response arrives in time. and when the benefits of new technology, such as artificial intelligence, is shared rather than hoarded and priced out of reach. It is restored when an embargo denounced in this chamber is finally lifted, when peace in a conflict is secured, and when a historical wrong is made right. Mr. President, we remain hopeful. With necessary changes in the organization and in the mindset of those of us who shape its work, the United Nations will live up to its name. However, we must manage this era of transformation with courage, honesty, and fairness, and including equally concerns of all the peoples of the world, who, despite our individual protestations, are inevitably part of our shared humanity. Thank you and may God bless us all.

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, Legal Affairs and Justice, Economic Planning and Private Sector Development of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Lord Va'afafina, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Tonga. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Mr. President, the General Assembly, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I bring you warm greetings from His Majesty King Tupou VI and the people of the Kingdom of Tonga. Nine months into my service as Prime Minister, I stand here mindful that Pacific leaders have come before me raising the same warnings, making the same appeals. Today, I'm compelled to make them again. The question before us is not whether the world has heard our message, but why has it still not acted? We live in a world more connected than ever, but greater connection has not brought greater unity. We meet amid deepening division, geopolitical conflict, and competition. For Tonga, navigating such stormy currents is not new. As descendants of voyagers, we have been in the survival business much longer than most have appreciated. Under King George I, Tonga preserved its independence during an era of colonial expansion. Our constitution of 1875 secured Tongans' rights and freedoms over seven decades before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It reflects our fierce determination to chart our own course. That is the essence of our sovereignty. Multilateralism allows us to project the power of our ideas rather than the might of our power. Tonga participates as an equal under the founding principles of the United Nations Charter. the sovereign equality of states. This is how we must approach our theme, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all. Enduring trust is restored when commitments produce results. True transformation is realized when our communities, economies, and ecosystems can anticipate change and recover with greater strength. The small and developing states must not bear the disproportionate costs of the challenges they did little to create. Mr. President, too much of our international architecture still reflects the world of 1945, rather than today's realities. If the United Nations is to remain the principal vehicle through which sovereign nations confront global challenges. It must transform. We need a United Nations that enables innovation, one that expands meaningful access to investment and technology, especially for the islands, developing countries, who are too often excluded from both. We need a stronger General Assembly and institutions that respond effectively to the needs of the majority of our members. We cannot keep negotiating climate, biodiversity, and the ocean in separate COPs when they are clearly an interconnected ecosystem requiring integrated and coherent solutions. We call on global processes to recognize the ocean climate nexus and address these interconnected challenges together. We need a more inclusive Security Council equipped for today's challenges, a Security Council that recognizes the triple planetary crisis as a profound threat to peace and security. We need a financial architecture that delivers timely and accessible financing to those who most need them. Internationally, pledged commitments must be actioned urgently. The next Secretary-General must understand these realities intimately. It is in this spirit that Tonga has nominated Ambassador Yvonne Baki of Ecuador, whose vision for a renewed, reformed United Nations speaks to the needs of vulnerable States. To restore trust, every Member State, large or small, must have a voice in shaping this organization's future and a stake in its success. Mr. President, Your Excellencies, the Pacific region spans one third of the Earth's surface. It is our home. Through the 2050 strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, we have set our own course and identified our thematic priorities. For Tonga, investing in the ocean and nature is foundational in achieving its development ambition. Protecting and restoring them builds our climate resilience. It strengthens our food security and enables a sustainable blue economy. The financing and partnerships we build around ocean and nature-based solutions will help determine our future and sustain our people. Mr. President, we have declared our region an ocean of peace in 2025. It sends a clear message. The Pacific must not become a staging ground for military escalation or a battleground for major power rivalry. However, our ocean of peace is more than the absence of conflict. Our most pressing threats are already reaching our shores. transnational crime, illicit drugs, illegal, unregulated and unreported fishing, cyber threats and unresolved consequences of nuclear testing and radioactive. contamination remain. In this respect, our region is committed to directly utilizing innovative technologies and working closely with our trusted security partners to address our security challenges. We are committed to protecting the rights of marginalized people and ending violence against women and young girls. This year, Tonga ratified United Nations Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities, reaffirming our commitment to the dignity and the equal participation of persons with disabilities. We also acceded to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. In doing so, we completed the universalization of the CTBT in the Pacific. On climate, the Pacific is already drowning in a crisis, a crisis that others continue to postpone addressing. UNEP's limiting overshoot report warns that exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius could occur within the next few years. But crossing that threshold must not become an excuse for abandoning it. We must peak as low as possible and return below 1.5 degrees Celsius as quickly as possible. Every fraction of a degree matters. The Pacific loses an estimated of $500 million every year due to natural disasters such as cyclones, flooding, Early warning systems give communities time to prepare and reduce these losses. That may be a modest sum in global terms, but for Pacific nations, it is a heavy toll on our countries and our people. And yet the financing to prevent such losses still falls short. The Pacific Resiliency Facility, our own financing mechanism for building community resilience, needs a further $328 million in pledges to reach its initial capitalization target of $500 million. Weather Ready Pacific, designed to reduce the human and economic costs of severe weather events, needs a further $160 million to reach its target. Tonga's Climate Trust Fund, a direct community fund which dispersed its first round of grants this year, also requires significant funding support. We call on all our partners to invest in these Pacific-designed and Pacific-owned solutions. Tonga stands behind 2026 Pacific Island Forum leaders. the Bilo Declaration, and calls on all our major emitters to act urgently. Climate action is a legal obligation, but meeting those obligations will require difficult decisions rooted in science. Climate leadership is not a popularity contest. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been breached by human activity. Climate inaction is not an option. Tonga is accelerating its transition away from fossil fuels and expanding renewable energy, and we encourage the shift to electric vehicles. For us, decarbonizing also means greater energy security and protection from global fuel price shocks. We must phase out the explicit fossil fuel subsidies estimated by the IMF at $725 billion. International financial institutions and multilateral development banks must recognize the multidimensional vulnerability index, the MVI, which ensures that it informs eligibility and allocations. By any credible index, Tonga is amongst the world's most vulnerable countries. However, we call on all nations, especially the world's largest emitters, to attend the pre-COP31 meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu in October this year. Come to the Pacific and confront what 1.5 degrees means for our water, our people, our food, our homes, and our security. We welcome the General Assembly's declaration on sea level rise, a significant achievement for the preservation of sovereignty. It marks the first time all member states have agreed on a single common text on sea level rise. Our resilience account for every hazard, including geo hazards confronting our islands. Over the last few years, Tonga has endured cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, and tsunamis. This year, the super El Nino currently forming over the Pacific Ocean further intensifies weather patterns, compounding the pressures on our people. We therefore need integrated warning and response systems that can protect our communities against the full range of planetary risks. Tonga has committed to protecting at least 30% of our ocean by 2030. Our ratification of the BBNJ agreement extends that commitment beyond our waters, supporting the protection of marine biodiversity on the high seas. Our task is to navigate a course that safeguards the ocean and unlocks its value to our people. This principle underpins Tonga's ocean strategy. It is in that spirit that we intend to convene a Polynesian Ocean Summit in Tonga, May of 2027, to move from shared ambition to practical action. But our responsibility does not stop at the boundaries of our Pacific continent. Consider the humpback whales. Born in Tonga's warm oceans, it migrates to Antarctica to feed on krill before returning to the Pacific to escape the winter and breed. Tonga's sanctuary protects them, but their survival depends on healthy ecosystems at both ends of that journey. What happens in the southern seas of Antarctica is felt in the southern oceans of Tonga. So we invite partners to join us in Tonga with practical commitments that recognize the scale and interconnectedness of our shared ocean corridors. Mr. President, the same principle extends across our development. Interconnection must not be dependency. For Tonga, resilience means taking greater control of the forces shaping our future and turning the resources within our geography into greater self-sufficiency. When we import fossil fuels, we also import their volatility. Moving away from them is therefore both a climate imperative and an energy security necessity. Tonga is not short of ambition. 70% renewable energy by 2030, 100% renewable energy by 2035. However, the forces shaping our future are not solely environmental or economic. They're increasingly technological. Mr. President, digital connectivity and rapid technology advancements are transforming how we live. They offer significant opportunities for both big ocean sovereign states, BOSS, but they also risk creating new inequalities and dependencies. Those who benefit last from global change often bear its highest costs. We continue to live with that injustice through climate change. We cannot again be asked to adapt only after systems have been built and the rules written. For Tonga, submarine cables and satellite links are foundational infrastructures that connect our islands to global opportunities. But connectivity alone is not enough. Digital skills and secure, resilient systems must support it. And we will protect our children online and retain sovereignty over our national data. Tonga does not need to be first in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, or every technology that follows. but Tonga will not simply endure global transformations. It will exercise sovereignty by helping shape the rules and norms around it. Tonga is looking beyond conventional development models. We are seeking to unlock new forms of finance through responsible valuation of our natural assets, our ocean assets, while exploring the potential of frontier technologies such as quantum science. We will form the right partnerships. We will direct innovation towards our priorities. But the Pacific's data ocean, biodiversity, critical minerals, and traditional knowledge must not power the next technological revolution while returning only a fraction of their value to our people. Mr. President, from experience, Tonga knows its challenges, and we will meet them with determination, that has always defined our people. We also know our strengths as a boss. We are not asking for charity. We will do our part. We will simply ask that others do this. Meet the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold. Help us protect the planet we all share and the ocean that connects us. Ensure that everyone benefits from technological advancements. Recognize the imbalance between the funds we commit to addressing our collective development challenges and those we are prepared to spend on conflict. Let's uphold the rules and institutions that allow every nation to participate as an equal sovereign. That is the promise at the heart of the United Nations. Not that all nations would be equal in power. but that no nation, however powerful, is more sovereign than another. That is the multilateral system Tonga believes in, an international rules-based order founded on the UN Charter and equality of nations. And that is the multilateral system we must preserve. Mr. President, I so submit. God bless us all. Malo e pito.

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Tonga. And now I give the floor to Her Excellency Moudipola Anarosa Ale Molio. Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance of Samoa. I ask the protocol to escort her Excellency to the podium.

O le atoa mo Samoa. O Samoa mo le atoa. Tapua i maia, malamanuia Samoa. Le atunuu pele. O le amomoli laumalilenga. President, let me begin by warmly congratulating His Excellency, Mr. Kalula Rahman, on his election as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly. The chosen theme for the General Debate, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nation that Delivers for All, could not be more timely. And it speaks to the reality of the world we face today. A world shaped by uncertainty, disruption, and rapid change, but also by hope, innovation, and opportunity. For Samoa, the theme is a promise the world must keep. Can trust be restored? Can transformation protect the vulnerable? The answer lies in the first words of our UN Charter, "We, the peoples." We must always put people at the center of our decisions. For us, this is underpinned by the core values of our Samoan culture, the fa'asamoa, and our faith, such as respect, dignity, love, protection, and service. Excellencies, every decision in this hall shapes the world that every child inherits. We meet at a pivotal moment in history. Profound and transformative changes are not only necessary, but inevitable. Across many societies, People are increasingly asking whether global institutions are delivering on the promises made to them. We must prepare ourselves to face the challenges ahead with resolve and use the opportunity to herald in much needed reforms for the benefits of all and leaving no one behind. For Samoa, Multilateralism remains the cornerstone of our international engagement. Only through genuine cooperation and mutual trust can we craft solutions that no single nation could achieve alone. The UN80 initiative has merits, but also its risks, if not fully assessed and understood. Any reform must strengthen delivery on the ground by eliminating duplication, improving coherence, and accelerating impact. Critically, such reforms must not weaken the operation of the UN multi-country offices or the resident coordinator system. We, Samoa, reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the United Nations As the premier forum to address global crisis, we also caution against premature decision taken without the full consideration and endorsement by member states. Excellencies, climate change remains the single greatest threat to Samoa and the global community. Its impacts are more extensively felt by SIDS due to our special circumstances. As the ICJ advisory opinion puts it, climate change is not merely an environmental concern, but an existential problem of planetary proportion that require urgent global action. The United Nations General Assembly welcome the unanimous ICJ advisory opinion and affirm its importance as an authoritative contribution to the clarification of existing international law. Climate finance is the bridge between ambition and action. It must be scaled up, easily accessible, devoid of burdensome condition, and responsive to the needs of the most climate vulnerable. Resources intended for education, Health, water and social protection are now diverted to disaster recovery. Small nations are being asked to finance both development and survival. No nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create. Excellencies, the world is facing a growing development financing crisis. The gap between commitments and delivery continues to widen. And too often, we simply rebrand and recycle old ideas while failing to deliver tangible progress. Meanwhile, multilateralism is under siege, and international financial commitments are being eroded. The current international financial architecture was designed for a different era. it struggles to adequately recognize vulnerability and fails to fully account for the realities faced by states. A fairer financial system is not only in the interest of developing countries, it is in the interest of global stability and shared prosperity. The implementation of the multidimensional vulnerability index, MVI, in financing decision making is essential if we are to genuinely address the financial challenges facing developing countries. We thank the Secretary General and UN DESA for their proactive efforts in moving this issue forward with international financial institution, IFIs. And we look forward to the pilot project to demonstrate that MBI can help developing countries in their financing challenges. On debt, we need to build a sustainable, equitable, and fair debt regime, starting with a robust mechanism for debt restructuring. Debt forgiveness must be linked to measurable progress on resilience building. and investment in resilience today will reduce the cost of disasters tomorrow. Samoa supports the incorporation of states contingent clauses in debt instruments, allowing for suspension during crisis. Excellencies, energy is both a driver and accelerator for Samoa's sustainable development ambition. Energy security has become a defining issue for many small island nations. While we have one of the highest shares of renewable electricity in the Pacific, Samoa remains heavily dependent on imported fuels. Successive energy crises and the 2026 fuel crisis exposed the economic cost of our energy dependence. We are working towards a whole of system transformation that delivers electricity that is reliable and affordable, reduces our dependence on imported fuels, strengthens resilience, and supports sustainable development. The clean energy transition is also an opportunity for Samoa to build a smarter, more resilient, and investment-ready energy system. The digital transformation, including AI and data analytics, offers real opportunities to drive an inclusive, just energy transition, particularly through off-grid solution and smarter energy planning. Excellencies, the ocean defines who we are as Pacific people. It connects us, sustains us, and shapes our identity. Yet our ocean faces increasing pressures from pollution, biodiversity loss, over-exploitation, and the impacts of climate change. Pursuing economic growth has come at a grave cost to our marine ecosystem. Coupled with unchecked exploitation of deep seabed mineral resources, our oceans face a crisis of limitless proportion. And these planetary changes have no middle ground. Weak governance frameworks threatens what remains. Without urgent action, small island states face a future without land and no usable ocean. It is time to transform how we value and interact with the ocean, from a resource we exploit to one we protect and cherish. and we must do more on this front. Samoa has ratified the BBNJ agreement, and we remain actively engaged in negotiations toward a global treaty on plastic pollution, particularly to protect our marine environment. We remain committed to implementing the Apia Commonwealth Ocean Declaration, the 2026 Pacific Island Forum Leaders Ocean Statements, and our own Samoa Ocean Strategy. These are critical to the implementation of SDG 14. Our maritime domain is increasingly exploited by transnational criminal networks involved in illegal trafficking, including illicit drugs moving through our region. Illicit drugs enter homes, harm young people, fuel violence, and place increasing pressure on communities and essential services. Excellencies, non-communicable disease represents one of the most serious development challenges to Samoa's public health and economic productivity. In response, we are shifting towards prevention through strengthening health literacy, reforming school nutrition and food environments, and early intervention programs. And this includes our Early Childhood Development Framework, a multi-sectoral roadmap to ensure every child from pregnancy to age five receives nurturing care, protection, and early learning. Excellencies. In many of our Pacific countries, our water systems are highly vulnerable to disruptions. These realities demand that the global water agenda fully recognize the special circumstances of SIDS. Samoa's priorities are fourfold. First, climate resilient water system must be scaled up urgently. Second, Access to finance must be significantly improved. And third, capacity and partnerships must be strengthened. And finally, we need a transnational water governance regime informed by the outcomes of the various water conferences held over the last eight years. Excellencies, Samoa remains a peaceful country. steadfast in our commitment to human rights and justice. We remain concerned by the ongoing wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran. The terrible loss of civilian lives, displacement of people, as well as the destruction of infrastructure and the environment is something we do not condone. The continued supply of weapons to fuel conflicts must end. We also reiterate our long-standing call for meaningful reform of the Security Council to ensure that it remains effective, credible, and representative of today's realities. It is imperative that the UN resolves disputes peacefully and strengthen international peace and security. The world needs a stronger commitment to peace. Not more division, not more conflict, and not more suffering. Excellencies, at its heart, Samoa's development journey is about investing in people. We are strengthening social protection, investing in youth, supporting women and persons with disabilities, and building a resilient economy. And these efforts are championed through our district development program, delivered across all 51 districts, empowering our communities. Our greatest source of resilience will not be our infrastructure or our institution alone. It will be our people, healthy, skilled, educated, and empowered. And this is why the aiga, or family, is at the heart of our pathway for the development of Samoa. Excellencies, I pay tribute to our outgoing Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, for his steadfast leadership and enduring commitment to the United Nations. His legacy will continue to guide our collective efforts in advancing peace, dignity, and sustainable development for all. Excellencies, before I am a leader, I am first and foremost a mother. History may record our titles, but our children will inherit our choices. And this is why, now more than ever, that United Nations matters. We must continue to stand as one United Nations family. God bless Soifua Ma'ia Manuia.
Thank you. I thank the Deputy Prime Minister of Samoa. And now I give the floor to His Excellency Geoffrey Huntley, Deputy Prime Minister of Saint Kitts and Nevis.

Mister President, Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, friends, and my fellow politicians and divisions at home and throughout the diaspora. I bring greetings from the proud twin federation, Island of Saint Kitts and Nevis. And our Prime Minister, the honorable Doctor Teron

Mr. President, we extend congratulations on your election as President of the 84th session of this Assembly. We also express sincere appreciation to your predecessor for her stewardship over the past year. I rise before this Assembly at a time when the world is not short of promises, declarations or commitments. What we need is proof that our institutions can respond to the realities people face. For small island developing states like ours, the question is immediate. Saint Kitts and Nevis therefore comes with a clear proposition Trust will be restored not by what we promise, but by what we deliver. The time has come to move from promise to proof. I come not only to speak about what the world must do, but to account for what we are doing. Mr. President, Last year, our Prime Minister, the honorable Doctor Terrence Drew, spoke of our sustainable island state agenda, Cesar. Our national blueprint for transforming Saint Kitts and Nevis into a more resilient, sustainable, inclusive, and prosperous society by twenty forty. Today, we return to demonstrate that it is becoming a record of delivery. Earlier this year, our second voluntary national review in the United Nations High-Level Political Forum showed stronger government coordination, close alignment with sustainable development goals, and tangible progress for our people. Water provides one of the clearest measures of that progress. One year ago, over 2 million gallon per day, solar power desalination plant was nearing completion. In February, we commissioned it. Through semi airborne drone surveys, we are also identified 17 new potential groundwater sources. and in August, completed drilling at the first rural site. Together with distribution upgrades, these investments are strengthening water security. In 2022, only 25% of our households had 24/7 water. Today, approximately 75% do. This is transformation. On the island of Nevis, we are advancing a 30 megawatt geothermal power development with drilling expected by early 2027 and Icelandic drillers contracted to begin the process. In Saint Kitts, Plans for a 50 megawatt solar PV and battery storage project are well advanced. These investments will reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen economic resilience. We are also strengthening food security to climate smart support for farmers and healthcare to our locally developed national digital health information system at the Joseph N. Franz General Hospital. Sustainability must be practical, people-centered, and built to last. Mr. President, there is more to do. But our experience proves that small states are not powerless. With investment, partnership, and political will, small nations can deliver big solutions. Saint Kitts and Nevis is not seeking pity. We are advancing partnership. A sustainable island state is not a distant ambition. We are building it today. Yet, even as we advance, the climate crisis is moving the goal post. This year, our federation and the wider Caribbean face severe drought. By the end of May, rainfall was 44% below the long-term average. We are investing in resilient infrastructure, but no small island developing state can adapt indefinitely to a crisis the world continues to intensify. Adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere. Distinguished colleagues, the science is unequivocal. The years 2015 to 2025 were the warmest on record. And in 2025, global average temperature remained about 1.43 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial baseline, while global mean sea level stood approximately 11 centimeters higher than in 1993. For island nations, this is a question of sovereignty and statehood. If our coastlines retreat, Our sovereignty must not. Mister President, climate induced sea level, rise must never erase a state's international legal personality. Extinguish its UN membership, deprive its people of nationality, or diminish lawfully established maritime zones of sovereign rights. The International Law Commission has laid foundations for continuity of statehood, sovereignty, maritime, entitlements. This assembly must turn them into firm guarantees. International law has spoken with the increasing clarity. Saint Kitts and Nevis welcome the International Court of Justice, advisory opinion on states climate obligations. Clarification must now become compliance. Compliments must become conduct. And promises must become performance. States must reduce emissions, strengthen adaptation, honor climate finance responsibilities, and cooperate with countries bearing consequences vastly disproportionate to their contribution to this crisis. Mister President, those contributions, lease, must not pay the greatest price. Our oceans must also move from promises to protection. Saint Kitts and Nevis ratified BBNJ agreement in twenty twenty-five. Implementation no matters. Large ocean states need access to capacity building, marine technology, scientific knowledge, and financing, while benefits from marine genetic resources must be shared fairly. For island nations, the ocean is not the space between us and the world. It is our highway, heritage, livelihood, and lifeline. Across climate action, sea level rise, and ocean governance, one reality remains: resilience has a cost. For decades, small island developing states have argued that income is not the same as resilience. Mr. President, per capita income cannot show exposure to hurricanes, droughts, pandemic, shipping disruptions, energy shocks, conflict or tourism collapse. Nor how quickly one shock can erase years of investment. This year, Saint Kate Sanibis stood before the United Nations and completed the pilot vulnerability and resilient country profile under the multidimensional vulnerability index framework. And what did we learn? We learned what our grandparents always knew. A house can look strong from the road and still have rot in the rafters. Vulnerability is not a statistic. It is the roof that was destroyed in Hurricane Beryl. It is the school that became a shelter. It is the family rebuilding for the third time in a decade because storms have no patience for GNI per capita. Mr. President, we are not asking that gross national income be discarded. We are asking that it stop being expected to tell a story it was never designed to tell. GNI can count our coconuts and our coolships. It cannot count our courage, and it cannot count the price we pay to simply remain. It cannot capture the cost of rebuilding the same bridge, clinic, or seawall again and again, while nations twice our size and half of our vulnerability borrow cheaper than we do. We therefore call on the World Bank, the IMF, development banks, climate funds, and every partner here to incorporate NVI into the architecture of financing. not as charity, but as arithmetic and justice made real. If vulnerability can be measured, it must be considered. Mr. President, the next great divide between nations must not be digital. Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities. St. Kitts and Nevis intends to participate. But we must ask who will shape this new age and who will live with decisions made elsewhere. At the end of 2025, some 2.2 billion people remain offline. But the AI divide also concern computing power, data research, skills, energy, cybersecurity, and capital. With the global AI market projected to reach US $4.8 trillion by 2033, developing countries cannot simply consume technologies designed and governed elsewhere. We must have a place where AI's future is decided. St. Kitts and Nevis welcomes the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Inclusion must lead to capability. Developing countries need affordable computing power, infrastructure, skills, and safeguards for privacy. data sovereignty, cyber security, and rights. Mister President, at home, we are advancing a whole of government technological strategy. Securing digital identity and digital public services. Regionally, the Caribbean AI Task Force supports cooperation and governance, innovation, and responsible adoption. Mr. President, artificial intelligence is already transforming the world. Saint Kitts and Nevis chooses to help shape that transformation. As SIDS, we know a simple truth. Alone, we are small. Together, we are formidable. The Caribbean Declaration as a zone of peace must retain its force as geopolitical competition moves closer to our shores. Our response must remain anchored in sovereignty, territorial integrity, international law, peaceful settlement of disputes, and diplomacy. CARICOM supports the International Court of Justice as the lawful path for resolving the Guyana-Venezuela dispute and the judicial process concerning Belize and Guatemala. We defend international law because, for small states especially, the alternative is a world where power becomes the rule. Across Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Chad, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, civilians continue to bear an unconscionable burden. St. Kitts and Nevis affirms one standard: international law applied consistently, not selectively, and conscience applied evenly, not conveniently. There can be no hierarchy of human suffering. Mister President, the future of multilateralism also depends on its leadership. Saint Kate Sanivis proudly joins Caricom in endorsing her excellency. Carolina Rodriguez Birket of Guyana for the office of the United Nations Secretary General. Her understanding of the challenges facing developing nations reflect the leadership this moment demands. Her candidature as an indigenous woman from a small developing state also reaffirms that global leadership must be defined not by the size of a nation, but by the vision, integrity, and capacity of those called to serve. Mr. President, few bridges carry greater historical meaning or future potential than between Africa and the Caribbean. The Atlantic, once a passage of forced displacement and separation, is becoming a pathway of return and reconnection. Africa Caribbean cooperation must move beyond sentiment. Our shared history must help build a shared future to capital, trade, technology, knowledge, culture, and coordinated diplomacy. Mr. President, South-South cooperation must be felt in jobs, businesses, knowledge transfer, and opportunity. It complements, not replaces, North-South cooperation and the obligations of developed countries. Greater accuracy must also include justice. At the second African Caribbean Summit, our leaders signed the Addis Ababa Declaration And this year, the African Union's Reparation Mechanism and the Caribbean Reparations Commission held their first joint meeting, establishing permanent coordination. On March 25, 2026, this General Assembly adopted Resolution 80/250 declaring that trafficking of enslaved African and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. Saint Kitts and Nevis welcome this historic recognition. But recognition cannot be the destination. Repertory justice must move from recognition to remedy and from words to action. Distinguished colleagues, when we speak of arbitrary justice, sovereignty and solidarity, Haiti cannot be an afterthought. Approximately 1.47 million people are internally displaced, while nearly half of the population faces acute food insecurity. In the very near future, the first round of presidential and legislative elections will take place. The Haitian people must choose their leaders freely, credibly, and safely. Mr. President, Saint Kitts and Nevis joins CARICOM in calling for the full deployment of the United Nations authorized Gang Suppression Force and the timely renewal of its mandate alongside Haitian-led recovery and governance. Mr. President, we remain deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation in Cuba. Saint Kitts and Nevis has contributed to humanitarian relief to the Cuban people and our own nationals studying there. We welcome the recent measures undertaken by the Cuban Government to improve the well-being of its people and encourage further meaningful action. We urge constructive dialogue between the Governments of Cuba and the United States, engagement Mutual respect and cooperation offers the best path improving the lives of the Cuban people and advancing peace and stability throughout our region. Mr. President, Saint Kitts and Nevis remains steadfast in its friendship with the Republic of China, Taiwan, and supports for its meaningful international participation. Earlier this year, we joined our Member States in requesting Taiwan's observer participation in the 79th World Health Assembly. We continue to support its meaningful participation in the World Health Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization, and other relevant mechanisms, and reiterate that differences across the Taiwan Strait must be resolved peacefully. Mr. President, no generation has a greater stake in our decisions than young people. Half of the world's population is under 30, yet 67 million young people were unemployed last year. and more than a quarter of a billion were neither in employment, education, nor training. AI, the green transition, and climate change are reshaping their future jobs. We must prepare them. Last year, our Prime Minister introduced this assembly to our Aspire program. Achieving success through personal investment, resources, and education. For citizens age 5 to 18. Built on savings, investment, and financial education, Aspire has opened more than 4, 000 savings accounts with our government committing more than US 2 million to give children a financial foundation for adulthood. We are now piloting our financial education curriculum in schools and training teachers for national rollout. We are not simply giving children money. We are giving them the knowledge to make money work for them. Financial independence must not be reserved for those born into wealth. Finally, Mr. President, Distinguished colleagues, for 81 years, this institution has represented a bold conviction that despite our differences, nations can come together around common rules, responsibilities, and human dignity. That conviction is worth defending. But institutions cannot live indefinitely on those founding promises. They must be judged by what those promises produce. Saint Kitts and Nevis remains ready to do its part and to work with every nation here towards a more peaceful, sustainable, equitable, and humane world. Mr. President, trust is not something we can demand. It must be earned by promising less, delivering more, and letting the proof speak where our words once stood alone. Let this assembly be remembered not for what was said here, but for what was done after. The tide is rising. Let our resolve rise faster still. Thank you.
Thank you. I thank the Deputy Prime Minister of Saint Kitts and Nevis. And now I give the floor to His Excellency, Abdulatif bin Rashid Al Zayani. Minister for Foreign Affairs of Bahrain.

In the name of God, the most gracious, the most merciful, Your Excellency, Dr. Khalil al-Rahman, President of the United Nations General Assembly. Your Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, ladies and gentlemen, peace and blessings of God be upon you. Allow me to congratulate you, Excellency, on your election as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly. I wish you every success in conducting the work of the session. We would like to express the Kingdom of Bahrain's appreciation to your brotherly country, the People's Republic of Bangladesh, as well as the Secretary-General for his tireless efforts in the service of international peace and security and the Sustainable Development Goals. It is my honor to convey to this distinguished gathering the greetings of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, and of His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, and their best wishes for the success of this session. Mr. President, you have chosen for this session a theme that speaks directly to the challenges before us, restoring trust, managing transformation, and a United Nations that delivers for all. Trust is not restored through statements or by repeating appeals. Instead, it is restored by upholding the law and translating the decisions of this organization into effective protection for people's lives, rights, and livelihoods. We meet at a time when the Arab Gulf is facing a security situation of a severity not witnessed in decades. The states of the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan have been subjected to waves of unjustified Iranian attacks involving ballistic missiles and drones, targeting civilian infrastructure, residential areas, ports, airports, and energy facilities. This came in flagrant violation of international law and the Charter of the United Nations. These are indiscriminate attacks without justification under any law. My country also condemns the attacks carried out by the Iran-backed terrorist Houthi militia against civilian objects and Islamic holy sites in the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We also condemn their threats to freedom of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb and the Red Sea. Allow me to put the facts before you in figures. Our countries have been subjected to nearly 7,000 attacks at the hands of Iran, involving 1,700 ballistic missiles, 80 cruise missiles and 5,220 drones. 2,000 cargo vessels and tankers with 20 1,000 seafarers on board have also been detained, while 72 commercial vessels have been targeted, resulting in the deaths of 22 seafarers. These are not merely numbers. Behind every figure is a ship, a port, a market, and families waiting for those that provide for them to return home. Commercial vessels have been targeted in the Straits of Hormuz. Mines have been laid in an international shipping lane. Restrictions on passage have been imposed in contravention of international law. The consequences of all the above extend far beyond the Arabian Gulf. It affects energy and food prices, shipping and insurance costs, as well as supply chains across the world. As the Kingdom renews its full solidarity with the brotherly countries subjected to these attacks, it commends the professionalism, of the Bahrain Defense Force and the air defense forces of brotherly countries and their readiness in confronting these attacks. We reaffirm the right of all states to take all lawful measures to defend their sovereignty and territorial integrity pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter and the Joint Defense Agreement of the GCC states. All the same, we continue to exercise the utmost restraint, seeking to ensure that security and peace prevail for the benefit of the people of the region. Mr. President, The position of the Kingdom of Bahrain is grounded in international law, the rights of peoples, and The Strait of Hormuz is an international strait and the right of transit through it is established for the vessels of all states under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. That right may not be suspended or obstructed, nor may it be subjected to conditions imposed unilaterally by any state. Accordingly, the Kingdom categorically rejects any permit or fee regime imposed on the passage. It rejects the use of international waterways as instruments of pressure or economic coercion, or any attempt at the seizure of vessels. Such actions would set an extremely dangerous precedent because what is accepted today in one strait may be demanded tomorrow in every international waterway upon which global trade depends. Alternative routes cannot be treated as a solution to conduct that violates international law. Mitigation measures are an emergency response. They should not be used as a pretext to claim that the strait is no longer necessary or to accept a new status quo. The right of passage does not cease to exist because alternatives are available, nor does a violation cease just because those affected have found ways to reduce the loss. This threat is not confined to the Strait of Hormuz. Security Council Resolution 2817 also referred to Bab el-Mandeb, recognizing that a threat to one waterway is a threat to navigation through all waterways. The security of navigation in the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Bab el-Mandeb is part of the same system. We are now not only defending a regional interest, but a rule that applies to every international waterway. And if it does apply to one, to our strait alone, it wouldn't have been a rule. The Kingdom of Bahrain has not only stated its position in principle on behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council states and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, and by virtue of its current presidency of the GCC and its non-permanent membership of the Security Council, Bahrain led efforts resulting in the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2817 with a historic and unprecedented support of 136 countries. The resolution condemned the attacks against our countries, reaffirming their sovereignty and rejecting any action intended to close the Strait or obstruct navigation through it. The Kingdom also introduced a draft resolution under Chapter VII of the Charter to protect commercial navigation. The resolution adopted by the Council of the International Maritime Organization on the 19th of March, together with the Human Rights Council Resolution 61/1, both have further demonstrated that the international rejection of such conduct extends beyond the Security Council. We stress the need for the full implementation of these resolutions. to ensure that those responsible are held accountable and there are compensation for the damage caused. On the 17th of this month, the Kingdom convened a reformula meeting of the Security Council dedicated to freedom of navigation. In this session, we heard from 53 affected states, the maritime transport sector and relevant international bodies And we heard a conclusion expressed by all delegations, that is, freedom of passage through international straits is a prerequisite for global economic prosperity. The Kingdom contributes to the protection of a rules-based maritime order across an area exceeding 3 million square miles through its hosting in Manama of the headquarters of the Combined Maritime Forces. This comprises 47 nations. We welcome the establishment of the Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance led by the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The Kingdom is proud to participate in the alliance as a founding member in support of efforts to safeguard international trade routes and global energy supplies in accordance with international law. As efforts continue in the Security Council, this General Assembly has an equally important role to play as the forum in which all States stand equal. From this podium, We call upon member states to support a firm collective position which upholds freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage in accordance with international law. It should also affirm that the security of maritime passages is a collective responsibility that cannot be subjected to bilateral arrangements. This is what restoring trust means in practice. This is not a call dictated by the present crisis. His Royal Highness Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, said from this very podium two years ago that the systems established to safeguard the international order were under severe strain. He noted that this organization must evolve to confront the growing threats. He called for comprehensive, consensus-based reform encompassing all decision-making bodies, including the Security Council. What has happened since then has not altered that conviction. Instead, it has reinforced it. Mr. President, the test of the United Nations' credibility is not only confined to our waters. The Palestinian cause remains at the heart of our concerns. The Kingdom reaffirms its steadfast position in support of the establishment of an independent and geographically contiguous state of Palestine living side by side with the state of Israel in peace and security. The Kingdom has also joined the Board of Peace as a founding member pursuant to Security Council Resolution 2803. This reaffirms our unwavering support for the rights of the brotherly Palestinian people. The Kingdom also reaffirms its support for the unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as for efforts to lift sanctions in a manner that enables the brotherly Syrian people to rebuild their country. In Sudan, we call for an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, and a political solution that preserves Sudan's unity and the state institutions. Turning to Yemen, we renew our support for a political solution under United Nations auspices led by the legitimate government. We appreciate the efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in this vein. Our position on other conflicts, including the conflict in Ukraine, is guided by the same principles, regardless of the parties involved. That is, adherence to the Charter, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain, where mosques, churches, and temples have stood side by side for generations, believes that tolerance and coexistence are not simply policies to be adopted. Instead, they are the identity of the Bahraini society and the foundation of our national unity. Thus, We have introduced the initiative adopted by the General Assembly, designating the 28th of January as the International Day of Peaceful Coexistence. His Majesty the King also issued the Kingdom of Bahrain's Declaration on Religious Freedom and Freedom of Belief. The King Hamad Global Center for Coexistence and Tolerance was later established, and the King Hamad Award for Coexistence and Tolerance was launched. The same approach underpins our development journey. The Kingdom continues to advance its Economic Vision 2030, pursue its commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and strengthen the status and advancement of Bahraini women. The Kingdom embraces the Women, Peace and Security agenda and the Youth, Peace and Security agenda, both our priorities during our membership in the Security Council. No discussion of development today is complete without addressing the technology that is reshaping that development. From this podium two years ago, His Royal Highness, the Crown Prince and Prime Minister, called for the adoption of an international treaty governing the development of artificial intelligence. It would ensure that this technology contributes to peace rather than exacerbating conflict. Since then, the General Assembly has taken positive steps. However, dialogue can bring positions closer, but it is not a step that creates obligations. The aim is not to hold the technology that no one has the power to hold, but to ensure that its growth is surrounded by safeguards, just as the international community surrounded Nuclear energy with safeguards that preserved its benefits without preventing it. This technology knows no borders. A safeguard adopted by a single state is not a safeguard, just as a rule that applies in a single strait is not a rule. Therefore, we renew our call for a binding international framework to ensure that this technology becomes a driver of innovation rather than division. And this, in our view, is what it means to manage the transformation that you chose as a theme of this session. Mr. President, all these issues, however far apart they may seem, are bound by one fundamental truth. Security and prosperity are not two parallel objectives. Instead, they are one single objective pursued along two paths. There can be no prosperity without security and no sustainable security without interconnected economies and societies in peace. This is not a Gulf perspective dictated by our geography. Instead, it's a lesson that humanity has learned from its wars, a lesson that Europe learned when it built its peace not through treaties alone, but on interests so intertwined that separating them became costlier than preserving them. It is in this light that we view freedom of navigation. A waterway is not merely a security issue of concern for coastal states. It is an artery of development through which the food, medicine, and energy of entire nations flow. When a single waterway is disrupted, the cost is felt by a family in a country that does not have a coastline. An economy that is difficult to disrupt is difficult to coerce, and interdependence, once firmly established, becomes a shield against coercion. This approach is not a position shaped by the current circumstances, it is what His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, has consistently advocated for out of His Majesty's conviction that the security and prosperity of this region are two faces of a single truth, and that a just peace and lasting stability are the path towards a dignified life for all the peoples of the region, their faiths or cultures. Thus, we reaffirm that what the United Nations needs today is not more resolutions, but greater capacity to implement them. A resolution adopted but not implemented has no value, and a right that is recognized but not protected has no value or meaning. I conclude by stating that the Kingdom of Bahrain continues to be guided by His Majesty's vision. For peace, as His Majesty sees it, is not declared, but built. It can rest only on the respect for human beings' dignities and beliefs. It should be built on dialogue, not concession. strength. The Kingdom will remain faithful to its international commitments and covenants, committed to international law, to freedom of navigation, and to a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace, true to His Majesty's approach and to to the conviction that the security of our region and the prosperity of its peoples are a shared responsibility that can only be safeguarded through our collective effort. We pray to Almighty God to grant this session every success and to bestow upon our peoples and all humanity security, peace, development, and prosperity. Thank you, and peace be upon you. Thank you.
I thank the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Bahrain. And now I give the floor to His Excellency Jeyhun Aziz Bayramov, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. At the outset, I warmly congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on assuming the presidency of the 81st session of the General Assembly and wish him every success in this important position. I also thank His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, for his endeavors. Ladies and gentlemen, as global challenges become increasingly complex, no country can address them alone. And yet, The growing limitations of multilateral mechanisms continue to undermine our collective ability to respond effectively to current and emerging threats. Meeting these realities requires joint action, but true transformation is impossible without first restoring trust in the international order and demonstrating that multilateralism can once again deliver tangible results for all. In an era marked by division, growing intolerance, and stark double standards, Azerbaijan advocates for a reinvigorated and reformed multilateral system underpinned by strict adherence to consistent and non-selective application of universally accepted norms and principles of international law. Azerbaijan supports a more effective UN capable of delivering tangible results for member states, especially in peace and security, development, climate resilience and humanitarian action. Through inclusive multilateralism, all states, large or small, particularly developing countries, must have the opportunity to participate equally in global decision-making. In this context, reform of the UN Security is essential to make it more representative, effective and responsive. Ladies and gentlemen, Restoring global trust begins first and foremost with respecting international law, sovereign equality, and peaceful coexistence. It is exactly these principles that are guiding our efforts for peace and stability in the South Caucasus. Even though the decades-long conflict with Armenia brought immense tragedy to our people and left deep scars across our land, Azerbaijan has chosen to look ahead and turn the page of enmity. We offered Armenia peace, fully in line with norms and principles of international law, based on mutual recognition of and respect for each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Our normalization efforts produced historic results at the Washington Peace Summit last August, where the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a joint declaration witnessed by President Trump of the United States of America. Through this declaration, both sides confirmed the end of the conflict and their will to jointly chart a peaceful and prosperous future. The sides also initialed the agreement on establishment of peace and interstate relations. Today, we have achieved de facto peace. Moreover, by unilaterally lifting transit restrictions, Azerbaijan facilitates transportation of goods to and from Armenia. We have also established bilateral trade. Azerbaijan provides strategically important oil products to Armenia on a regular basis, despite increased volatility in markets and growing international demand for these commodities. As we proceed with the peace agenda initiated by Azerbaijan, our entire region is now turning into a promising anchor of stability, connectivity, and tangible economic dividends. To make this process irreversible, it is of crucial importance to eliminate the remaining obstacle which will allow finalization of the normalization process through the signing of the already initialed bilateral agreement. Excellencies, complementing the regional normalization process, Azerbaijan's post-conflict rehabilitation agenda aims to ensure that hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis can eventually exercise their right to a safe and dignified return to their homes. Due to large-scale reconstruction efforts taken by the government, life is now returning to our liberated territories. Azerbaijan is rebuilding the entire region through smart cities and smart villages powered by green technology. Areas that were once rubble and ashes are now rising as modern settlements. Today, more than 90,000 people live, study, and work in the liberated territories. Regretfully, a massive contamination of the territories of Azerbaijan with landmines and other explosive devices remains a serious obstacle. This significantly obstructs the reconstruction and return process. Since the liberation of occupied territories in 2020, more than 400 individuals, including women and children, became victim to landmines. The cumulative toll of landmines over the past 30 years exceed 3,500 people. Given the scale of the problem, Azerbaijan considers mine action an essential prerequisite for fulfilling human rights and has formally declared humanitarian demining its 18th national sustainable development goal. Similarly, the need to clarify the fate and whereabouts of nearly 4,000 Azerbaijanis who went missing due to the conflict is essential. not only for accountability and the rights of the victims and their families, but also for post-conflict reconciliation and normalization. Mr. President, in the face of increasingly complex global challenges, our collective response must be inclusive, equitable, and universal. Azerbaijan's own experience reflects these principles. Our society is inherently multicultural and multiconfessional, shaped by centuries of peaceful coexistence of diverse ethnic, cultural, and religious communities. This tradition is reflected in Azerbaijan's international initiatives, including the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue. Launched in 2008 in the framework of the Baku Process, the Forum has evolved into a prominent global platform for advancing intercultural dialogue and cultural diversity. receiving international recognition, including through a series of United Nations General Assembly resolutions. Building upon these values, under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, His Excellency Mr. Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan has taken important steps to strengthen international solidarity, to build bridges, and to mobilize collective responses. This commitment has also been demonstrated through successful hosting and steering of major global gatherings, including COP29, the 13th session of the World Urban Forum, results-oriented chairmanships of the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organization of Turkic States, and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, and Azerbaijan's increasingly active engagement across other international platforms. Azerbaijan's full-fledged membership in the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and the C6 format will enhance our contribution to cooperation and connectivity within the region and beyond. COP29 provided a good example of this approach in practice. As host and presidency, Azerbaijan guided negotiations toward ambitious and balanced outcomes, while working to ensure that all voices were heard. The conference delivered several historic agreements, including the tripling of the global climate finance goal, full operationalization of Article 6 carbon market mechanisms, and further advancement of arrangements supporting the loss and damage fund for vulnerable communities affected by climate change. Our efforts to advance climate action likewise did not end with COP29. Azerbaijan continues to build on its legacy with particular focus on translating negotiated outcomes into practical implementation. This September, for the first time, Baku hosted the UNFCCC Climate Week, bringing together governments, international organizations, the private sector, and other stakeholders to advance implementation and practical solutions. Azerbaijan's commitment to international solidarity and cooperation is equally reflected in our development and humanitarian assistance. In recent years, Azerbaijan has significantly expanded the scope of its international aid, with particular attention to small island developing states and African partner countries. Since 2020, we have provided humanitarian, economic, and technical assistance worth approximately USD 400 million to more than 140 countries. As we mark the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, Azerbaijan reaffirms its commitment to partnership-based approaches founded on solidarity, mutual respect, and shared development priorities. Ladies and gentlemen, as we inch closer to 2030, it is becoming even more apparent that the world remains off track in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals. Azerbaijan is firmly committed to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, having integrated the SDGs into its national development strategies, institutional frameworks, and voluntary national review processes, while placing particular emphasis on connectivity, green growth, digitalization, and sustainable urban development. In less than two decades, Azerbaijan's GDP has increased threefold, while the poverty rate has declined from 49% to around 5%. At the same time, Azerbaijan maintains one of the lowest levels of public external debt globally. Our commitment also extends to advancing sustainable development through effective and accountable institutions. At Azerbaijan's initiative, on 30 March 2026, the UN Human Rights Council adopted by consensus for the third time

Resolution entitled Promoting Human Rights and the Sustainable Development Goals through Transparent, Accountable, and Efficient Public Service Delivery. Co-sponsored by more than 100 member states, the resolution underscores the essential role of citizen-centered, transparent, and efficient public institutions in advancing human rights and accelerating progress toward the SDGs. Azerbaijan's innovative ASAN and DOS models of transparent, accessible and citizen-centered public service delivery have gained international recognition and are increasingly being adopted by dozens of partner countries. Sustainable urbanization is another important pillar of our approach to the 2030 Agenda. Resilient cities are essential to improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and promoting inclusive economic and social development. In this context, Azerbaijan's successful hosting of the 13th session of the World Urban Forum marked an important contribution to the global urban agenda. The key outcomes of the forum, the Baku Call to Action and the Chair's Summary subsequently contributed to the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on mid-term review of the New Urban Agenda held in New York in July this year. At the same time, environmental protection remains an important national and regional priority. We are particularly concerned by continuing decline of the Caspian Sea with serious implications for biodiversity, livelihoods, and economic activity across the region. As a challenge shared by all Caspian littoral states, it requires a coordinated, collective, and sustained response. Excellencies, While remaining firmly committed to our climate goals, we must also recognize that in the immediate term, development cannot realistically proceed without traditional energy sources. Energy security, moreover, is closely intertwined with peace, regional connectivity, and sustainable economic development. As a reliable natural gas supplier to 16 countries, Azerbaijan ranks among the leading pipeline gas suppliers globally and plays a strategic role in strengthening energy security and diversifying supply routes across Europe and beyond. Azerbaijan's contribution to global energy security is increasingly complemented by its growing role in the clean energy transition. We are investing in renewable energy, commissioning major solar and wind projects, expanding hydropower capacity, and developing new clean energy initiative together with leading international partners. Agreements already signed envisage around 6 gigawatts of additional solar and wind capacity by 2030. By 2030, renewables are expected to generate almost 40% of Azerbaijan's electricity. Expansion of renewable power generation will create new opportunities for Azerbaijan to export green electricity to European markets. This way, Our role as a reliable energy partner is evolving alongside the global energy transition. Energy connectivity is part of Azerbaijan's broader vision of connecting regions, markets, and economies. Azerbaijan has emerged as a key transport and logistics hub between Europe and Asia, contributing to major transregional connectivity initiatives, investing in modern transport infrastructure, and expanding cooperation with regional partners. Since 2022, we have witnessed an increase in cargo volumes along the Middle Corridor by almost 90%. Strategic infrastructure projects along the Middle Corridor, spearheaded by Azerbaijan, including the Baku International Sea Trade Port and the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, are helping to create more resilient, diversified, and sustainable supply chains between Asia and Europe. This growth demonstrate the Middle Corridor's considerable potential as a key driver of regional connectivity, trade facilitation, and sustainable economic development. Our connectivity agenda extends beyond energy and transport. Digital connectivity offers another important area for regional cooperation. Azerbaijan is advancing new digital links across the region through ambitious initiatives such as the Digital Silk Way. This project envisages an advanced fiber optic network across the Caspian Sea, further strengthening Azerbaijan's role as a regional digital hub and a key link between Europe and Asia. This broader connectivity agenda is also closely linked to the emerging peace architecture in the South Caucasus. Our collective inability to prevent conflicts, our collective indifference toward humanitarian crisis, and our collective reluctance to seek common solutions to shared challenges are all becoming normalized. Trust cannot be restored when international law is applied selectively and commitments remain unfulfilled. Our response must be grounded in the fundamental values we have affirmed together: freedom, equality, justice, and respect for human dignity. But to fill its potential, UN must be able to act, adapt and deliver. We fully support the UN80 initiative. The success of the reform should be measured not by what is cut or reorganized, but by whether the United Nations prevents conflicts more effectively, responds more rapidly to crisis and delivers better results for all member states. Central to this renewal is reform of the Security Council. Equitable geographical representation must apply throughout the United Nations system as a condition of legitimacy and credibility. And Kazakhstan supports a transparent, inclusive, and merit-based process conducted in full accordance with the Charter. Mr. President, the international security environment continues to deteriorate. World military expenditures reached a record 2.9 trillion dollars in 2025. Our small planet is home to more than 12,000 nuclear weapons, each one capable of untold damage and sorrow. Every year we seem to lose more biodiversity, yet gain more armaments. For Kazakhstan, nuclear disarmament in particular is not an abstract doctrine. It's a responsibility born on the national experience. This year marks 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, 30 years since the CTBT opened for signature, and 20 years since the signing of the SIPRI-Palatins Treaty on nuclear weapon-free zone in Central Asia. Our experience of re-announcing the world's fourth largest nuclear arsenal did not weaken our state. To the contrary, through international trust, it strengthens sovereignty, enhances security, and promotes development. Today, the trust is again in danger. New START has expired, while the 2026 NPT Review Conference ended without substantive outcome for the third consecutive cycle. Nuclear weapons states must never confuse the absence of agreement with a vacuum of obligation. They remain responsible until we secure a world free of nuclear weapons.
