He will be remembered as a leader with a steady hand, always guided by principles of fairness, compassion, and dignity for all. Mr. President, the United Nations has now completed the first eight decades of its existence. Eight decades replete with resolutions, declarations, and action on decolonization, development, new international order, the new constitution for the oceans, as well as climate and the environment, technology, human rights, international law, and peacekeeping. Created in the aftermath of the Second World War, The immediate focus was obviously on peace and security, but the UN system has evolved significantly over the decades to expand its scope and sphere of influence within the confines of its charter. However, the UN must now look to the future, building on its record of achievements, as well as from lessons learned from what it could not achieve. As we look to the next 80 years, we must ask ourselves a searching question. Is the UN fit for the purpose for the 21st century, not the world of 1945, but the world of today and beyond? We are entering a new era of international relations defined by unprecedented technological developments, often absent from the table where the rules of tomorrow are being adopted. developing countries risk being left further behind. The same exclusion afflicts the international financial architecture, which remains skewed against the Global South. Developing nations must have a seat at the table as equal stakeholders. We all acknowledge that the three pillars of the UN Charter are peace and security, development, and human rights. The twin institutional pillars provided in the Charter were and still are the Security Council and ECOSOC as the apex bodies for achieving these purposes. However, over the years, optimal use has been made primarily of only one of these organs. We need to enhance and accelerate the revitalization of the General Assembly and that of ECOSOC so that they are not merely forums for debate but engines of action. This must be done as we bring about the reform of the Security Council. The historical injustice regarding the composition of the Council was acknowledged in Action 39 of the Pact for the Future, but the process for reform is still stalled. Mauritius fully supports the common African position the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sertic Declaration, calling for no fewer than two permanent and five non-permanent African seats on the Council. Mauritius also supports the call for SIDS to have a seat on a reformed Council. On the question of the veto, Mauritius aligns itself with the position of a growing number of states that in the event the veto is retained, Any new permanent member must have the same rights as the original permanent members. Mauritius also supports the Franco-Mexican initiative on the suspension of the veto in cases of mass atrocities. We support the positions of the G4 and the L69 on Council reform, and we reiterate our support for India's candidature for a permanent seat. commensurate with its constructive role in global affairs. Mr. President, Mauritius welcomes the increasing recourse to the International Court of Justice as a mechanism for the peaceful settlement of disputes and determination of issues of international law. We call upon member states which have not yet done so to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ. We welcome the landmark unanimous advisory opinion of the ICJ on the obligations of states in respect of climate change. This was a vindication of the tireless advocacy of Vanuatu and the core group of states. Mauritius was proud to stand among them. We call for the full operationalization of this advisory opinion, including through the follow-up action requested by this Assembly, in accordance with the UN General Assembly landmark resolution of the 20th of May 2026, welcoming the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice on the obligations of states in respect of climate change. We also support the legal principle affirmed by the ICJ that states are under no obligation to update the maritime baselines or zones to account for climate-induced sea level rise. Mauritius calls for the principle that statehood and sovereignty are not impacted by sea level rise to be formally codified. Mr. President, water stands at the frontline of the climate crisis. Water is a major concern globally. and Mauritius welcomes the holding of the UN Water Conference in December this year. We look forward to this crucial global issue being addressed by the international community as a matter of urgency. We also call for enhanced, accessible and predictable climate finance accompanied by comprehensive capacity building and disaster risk management for the most vulnerable. I also wish to highlight that Mauritius is currently conducting a constitutional review exercise, which will include giving constitutional protection to the rights of nature. Mr. President, the crisis in development financing is deepening. Concessional financing for developing countries is declining precisely when the need is greatest. The graduation of countries, including small island developing states, should be encouraged and supported and not prejudice access to affordable finance. Mauritius calls for a review of the criteria for access to concessional financing that reflect vulnerability rather than income per capita alone. We also call for the strengthening of the rules-based multilateral trading system and for fair, transparent and equitable mechanisms for resolving trade disputes. Mr. President, the rapid evolution of digital and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, is already shaping economic, social and institutional developments across the globe. We support the General Assembly resolution establishing the global dialogue on AI governance and welcome the work being done by the independent international scientific panel on AI. For Mauritius, digital innovation is a developmental imperative. We have launched, with UN support, a national artificial intelligence strategy and a national fintech strategy. We need an open, transparent and inclusive dialogue on governance of the new technologies, which ensures that the benefits of technological progress are shared equitably and that the risks are managed collectively. As a coastal state with an EEZ of 2.2 million square kilometres, that is more than 1,000 times our landmass, Mauritius is profoundly connected to the ocean. reaffirm our unwavering commitment to UNCLOS as the legal framework governing all activities in the oceans, including the seabed and subsoil beyond national jurisdiction. We welcome the decisions of the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf approving the submission lodged by Mauritius in December 2008 and approved in March 2011, as well as the second one filed in May 2009 and approved in July 2026. We welcome the 100th ratification of the BBNJ Agreement and calls for its prompt and effective implementation. We look forward to its first conference of the parties advancing the institutional financial and procedural arrangements necessary for the effective implementation of the agreement. Collaboration is key to effective maritime security, maritime surveillance and domain awareness. We call on the international community to support regional and sub-regional initiatives in this regard. I am pleased to inform that Mauritius will, with the support of the European Union and the Commission de l'Ocean Indien, will host a ministerial conference on cybercrime and sea cable security in the Western Indian Ocean in the first quarter of 2027. Mr. President, Mauritius welcomes the major developments taking place across Africa with regards to greater integration and pooling of resources, particularly in relation to capacity building. In this regard, Mauritius has initiated action at the UN for promoting enhanced regulatory frameworks in developing countries, namely through pooling of resources. Mauritius attaches great importance to the elimination of all forms of racism, racial discrimination and xenophobia. We welcome the high-level meeting on this subject and reaffirm our commitment to the international decade for people of African descent. Mauritius is fully committed to supporting the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. Earlier this year, Mauritius adopted new legislation to further enhance the protection of women's rights. Mr. President, we are deeply concerned by the effects of regional conflicts and instability on development, economic growth, food security, and achievement of SDGs. The crisis in the Gulf and threats to freedom of navigation have sent shockwaves across the global economy. For small open economies such as Mauritius, which depends on maritime trade routes for over 90% of its primary energies imports, and more than 70% of its food supply, these effects are felt acutely. We call for restraint, for dialogue, and for a durable diplomatic resolution. On Palestine, Mauritius reaffirms its long-standing position in support of the inalienable right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and to an independent, sovereign state with East Jerusalem as its capital, living in peace and security along its neighbors. The cycle of violence must end. Too many people have suffered for far too long. We note with deep concern that the establishment of unlawful settlements may be a major obstacle to peace. Mr. President, I now come to an issue which for Mauritius is non-negotiable. It concerns our sovereignty over the Chagos Islands. The agreement on the Chagos Archipelago, signed by Mauritius and the United Kingdom in May 2025, stands as living proof that trust in multilateralism and UN judicial organs can achieve the peaceful settlement of disputes and the completion of our nation's decolonization and restore the rights of Mauritians of Chagos origin by force of law. Trust, especially amongst neighbors and in the region, is reinforced when there is respect for the rule of law for the resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly, the ruling of the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea, and the ICJ's advisory opinion on the Chagos Archipelago, which carries authoritative obligations. We trust that states which laid the very foundation of the new post-war legal order will recommit to full respect and compliance with international law and correct this historical injustice without delay. As William Edward Gladstone, a full term former British Prime Minister and great campaigner for peace and freedom, put it, justice delayed is justice denied.

Mr. President. Tromelin Island is an integral part of the territory of the Republic of Mauritius. We have constantly maintained our position concerning the sovereignty of the Republic of Mauritius over this island. We reiterate our call upon France to engage constructively with a view to resolving the dispute relating to Tromelin Island. in the spirit of friendship which characterizes relations between our two countries.

Mr. President, Mauritius is committed to upholding the pledges made at the Social Summit in Doha last year. Nowhere is that promise to universal social protection more concrete than in our health services. As non-communicable diseases and a rapidly aging population place growing pressure on our health system, We are strengthening public healthcare through major investment, improved service delivery, expanded specialised care, and a greater focus on prevention. Mauritius will continue to offer free and quality public healthcare to each and every citizen. We thus welcome the holding of the 2027 High-Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage, and Mauritius stands ready to contribute to that global effort. Today, the high-level meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response met at a decisive moment. And decisive moments demand more than mere intentions. Mauritius supports the conclusions of the terms of benefit sharing guaranteeing vulnerable countries real access to affordable, safe, effective, and quality medicines including generics, vaccines, diagnosis, diagnostics and health technologies. It is of crucial importance to widen pandemic financing eligibility including the pandemic fund to formally incorporate the multi-dimensional vulnerability index. Mauritius also welcomes UN initiatives on roof on road safety. An issue to which we are touched the highest importance. And which acts as a silent epidemic that continues to claim far too many lives, disproportionately in developing countries. We call for greater international attention and resources for this critical issue.

Mr. President, we find ourselves at a critical juncture in the history of the United Nations. The organization is facing significant challenges, both internally and externally. Internally, there is the process launched by the Secretary-General to update the administrative and financial structure of the Organization to allow our Organization to be better equipped to overcome future challenges. Externally, the role and the functions of the Organization, as well as the composition of its principal organs, are in doubt and need to be redefined. The will expressed by the international community following the war to create an instrument for cooperation in order to establish a new world order is still there. The fact that the number of actors has more than tripled in the past eight decades reflects an engagement and a commitment that is even bigger and even more diverse than it was when the UN was created. We are confident that the international community, around half of which is made-up of young people that aim to protect the planet, that want to better share wealth, and aspire to use new technologies advisedly, will be able to overcome new challenges. We reiterate our commitment to multilateralism. as well as our confidence in its ability to respond to people's expectations. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration and International Trade of Mauritius. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Abdul Majid Abdul Rahim Mohamed Minister of Public Health and Prevention of Chad.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, heads of state and government, Secretary-General of the United Nations Organization, Distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, the Marshal of Chad, Mahamat Idriss Deby Ino, President of the Republic, Head of State, who, because of pressing national issues, has given me this great honor of representing him and conveying his message to you at this august assembly. Mr. President, your election at the presidency of the 81st session of the General Assembly of our shared organization bears witness to the trust that the international community has placed in you and in your leadership. Please be assured of the full support of the Republic of Chad as you carry out your term. I would also like to thank Madam Annalena, outgoing president of the General Assembly, for heading up the work of the 80th regular session so brilliantly. At a time when he is preparing to move on from being the head of our organization, I would like, ladies and gentlemen, to pay a very sincere tribute to the Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres. His leadership and constant commitment to peace, conflict prevention, and multilateralism warrant our recognition and respect. Chad is grateful to him for his ongoing attention to the challenges that our country, the Lake Chad Basin, and Central Africa are confronted with. Mr. President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, We are here today at a unique moment in the history of our organization. At a time when the UN is discussing crucial reforms and multilateralism is at a crossroads, the topic of this 81st session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, is a very relevant topic. It summarizes the expectations of member states and the peoples of the world in all of their diversity vis-a-vis the UN. Each year, we adopt new resolutions and we reaffirm our commitments. Each year, we renew our faith in multilateralism. Nonetheless, conflicts persist. People are still awaiting justice. Will generations still grow up with fighting as their backdrop? Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Security Council reform illustrates alone this situation and this crisis of confidence. For decades now, positions have been well known, calls for reform have stacked up, and consultations have multiplied. but progress still remains insufficient. Chad reiterates to this end its complete support for the common African position, as stipulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirt Declaration, and taken up in the African model for reform of the Security Council, presented in April by Sierra Leone on behalf of the Committee of Ten of the African Union. Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Chad considers that those difficulties facing multilateralism stem in part from the cynicism of the most powerful and from double standards policies. My country remains committed to multilateralism that is based on the UN Charter, the sovereign equality of states, the respect for their independence, cooperation and international solidarity. Thus, the government of the Republic of Chad, on the 27th of July, 2026, informed the Secretary General of the United Nations as its depository of its sovereign and irrevocable decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. This decision follows an in-depth consideration of how the court has functioned since it was set up in 2002. The data provided by the court and the lessons learned from that have shown us that in several states and among their populations, one can detect that the focus of the judicial activity of the court is on developing countries and in particular on Africa, which has become the target of political instrumentalization. I'd like to be perfectly clear here. This choice does not mean we are renouncing our responsibilities, nor are we becoming a refuge against justice, and even less so are we being complacent in the face of impunity. We will continue to strengthen our national courts and support credible, independent and effective African mechanisms that can protect victims and prosecute the perpetrators of the most serious crimes. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, nationally speaking, by the grace of God and thanks to the maturity of its people, Chad remains a country of peace and stability, despite the numerous domestic challenges it faces and the crises that threaten its borders. The President of the Republic, the Marshal of Chad, Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, as guarantor of these institutions, remains determined to maintain peace, to build national cohesion, and to create conditions for sustainable shared development. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, today, countries in the South are feeling the full brunt of climate change. Lake Chad is one of the most salient symbols of this, Its being vulnerable directly affects the means of subsistence of millions of people. We would therefore urge developed countries to uphold their commitments in terms of adaptation, resilience, loss and damages and technology transfer financing. Mr. President, the clear ambition that my country has for its development can only be achieved with peace, stability and security in our region and also in the world. The security situation in the Sahel and in the Lake Chad Basin demands our constant attention. Terrorist groups in the Lake Chad Basin, albeit weakened, continue to plunge our countries into mourning. Regarding Libya, Chad is delighted that the dialogue under the auspices of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General of the UN has been resumed, whilst hoping for a swift settlement of the dispute. In the Central African Republic, Chad has discreetly and consistently striven for mediation. This led on the 19th of April 2025 to the signature of a ceasefire agreement between the Central African Republic government and two of the main armed groups of the country. More recently in Haiti, Chad responded to the call from our organization. We decided to deploy 1,500 service personnel to the Gang Suppression Force authorized by the Security Council, and that is about a quarter of the planned amount. Through its constant vision for years now, Chad has remained one of the main African contributors of troops to peacekeeping operations throughout the world. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, This solidarity that we project outwards is something we also experience every day within our own borders. Since April 2023, more than a million Sudanese refugees have crossed our eastern border, fleeing a bloody conflict. Along with displaced persons from other regional crises, my country is currently hosting more than 2 million people who've been forcibly displaced. One person out of 17 in my country is today a refugee. From this rostrum, I would like to solemnly reiterate and reaffirm Chad's position regarding the Sudanese conflict. Our country has observed since the very first day of the war, strict, absolute and unchanged neutrality. I would like to say this very firmly. My country does not support any of the parties to the conflict in Sudan and in no way authorizes the use of its territory or its infrastructure to their benefit. Chad reiterates its commitment to peace in Sudan. and reiterates its support for all initiatives, including those of the Quad and the Quintet, seeking to establish a ceasefire and to promote dialogue between the warring parties. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I cannot now remain silent regarding the serious nature of that which is directly affecting our sovereignty. Over recent days, the Energy East province within our country has been the theatre of air strikes linked to the conflict in Sudan. Chad condemns in the strongest possible terms these new incursions. They are an unacceptable violation of our territorial integrity, and Chad reserves the right to take all necessary measures in line with international law to protect its population and its sovereignty if this occurs again. Mr. President, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I would also from this rostrum like to stress how concerned my country is with the crisis in the Gulf region and the repercussions of this on the global economy. Loyal to the principles of the Charter, Chad rejects any act of aggression against a sovereign State and condemns, to this end, the air strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran and, along the same lines, Chad very firmly condemns the Iranian attacks against the fraternal countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council and Jordan, as well as the drone attack on 29 July in the Egyptian port of Damietta. We would urge all parties to demonstrate restraint and to promote dialogue. Regarding the Middle East, Chad remains seriously concerned by ongoing violence and humanitarian suffering in Gaza. Sticking to its unwavering position, my country reiterates its unfailing commitment to the right of the Palestinian people to have their own state in the 1967 borders, alongside a state of Israel that lives in peace and security. As we do each year on this same occasion, we call once again for the lifting of the economic and trade embargo imposed on Cuba and on its people. Mr. President, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation. first and foremost requires consistency between what we declare here and what we do when the microphones are turned off. The choices that Chad makes, the responsibilities that it shoulders, and the sacrifices that it makes all stem from the belief that multilateralism only has a future if it knows how to reform, if it can correct any imbalances, and if the same principles can be applied to all. Chad remains firmly committed to the ideals that prevailed at the time of the establishment of the United Nations. Despite disappointments, we still believe in the force of law against the right to use force. We believe in a more representative organization of the world as it is now, more effective in its work, and truly delivering for all. Long live international cooperation. Long live Chad. I thank you.
I thank the Minister of Public Health and prevention of child. I now give the floor to His Excellency Espen Barth Eide, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway.

"The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born. Now is the time of monsters." President, distinguished delegates, these words stem from the Italian philosopher Antonio Gramsci, written in one of Mussolini's prison cells in the 1930s. The monsters he refers to were the dark political, social and ideological phenomena of his time. Gramsci describes a time of transition, of insecurity and the collapse of hegemonies. His worries were not unwarranted. His era ended with the largest catastrophe of them all, the Second World War. Our United Nations was founded by leaders who had lived through two world wars a devastating economic collapse, and the rise of fascism and Nazism. They had experienced firsthand that all nations suffer in war and conflict and when international cooperation fails. We, too, are living in turbulent times. Yet, at the very moment when we need it most, our United Nations faces its most serious challenge. We see an erosion of respect for international law, a loss of confidence in the merits of cooperation, of financing, and of effectiveness. These are symptoms of the same disease, a growing belief that power matters more than principle, a growing temptation to seek national advantage at the expense of common rules. But history teaches us a simple lesson. When rules are undermined, instability grows. When cooperation weakens, instability spreads. Smaller countries like my own, and in fact the vast majority of this Assembly, are particularly dependent on common international rules. But we also learned that all states end up suffering if unchecked violence is unleashed. Today, the repercussions of ongoing wars are felt across the globe. I am here with one message. We who honor the UN Charter must also stand ready to make some tough calls. Reform is necessary. Not because the United Nations failed, but because it matters. President, today, our United Nations finds itself in a triple crisis. It's a normative crisis. is a financial crisis and an institutional crisis. First, the normative crisis. The fundamental rules that protect the integrity of sovereign state and prohibit the use of force except in self-defense are threatened. The number of ongoing wars is alarmingly high. Most dramatically, the number of wars between states is the highest since the United Nations was established. Yet, this was the key motive for establishing this organization in the first place, to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. International law is not charity to the weak. It's a common investment in a system that reduces risk, friction, and cost for everyone, including the great powers. Take freedom of navigation as an example. This long-standing principle enshrined in our Convention on the Law of the Sea benefits every state. The Strait of Hormuz shows us why. Its closure raises energy prices, disrupts global supply lines, and curbs growth far beyond the region itself, from petrol pumps in Minneapolis to Oslo, from Cape Town to Mumbai. International law is not a menu you can choose from at will. It must be upheld universally. When we condemn Russia's clear violation of international law in Ukraine, it is equally important to speak out of Israel's violations of the same rules in Palestine. International law is only relevant if it's enforced. There is no alternative to the two-state solution. At this General Assembly, there has been a record number of Palestine-related meetings. The support for a Palestinian state has never been stronger, yet the situation on the ground is more dire than ever. We must act now with moral clarity and ensure that the coming year becomes a year of implementation. My message is this. Only if we apply international law to all people, in all places, and at all times, can we claim that these are universal rules. Double standards, quickly translate into no standards at all. Secondly, the UN is in a financial crisis. Major contributors are withholding or delaying payments. Wars and security concerns divert resources away from the fulfillment of our sustainable development goals. And when resources are available, they too often come with strict earmarking. We, the donors, should earmark less and allow more flexible use of resources. Norway remains one of the UN's 10 largest donors. We will use our funding to support and promote reform because we believe in investing in the UN. We believe that active, constructive implementation of the UN agency reforms is necessary for its future. This will be a key factor when we assess future voluntary contributions to agencies, funds and programs. Thirdly, the UN is in an institutional crisis. I am a strong believer in this organization, but I also recognize that over time, we have added excessive complexity to our United Nations. Too often, when we identify a new challenge or a new idea, we create a new agency, a new convention, a fund or a program to address it. Which then comes with secretariats, staff, resources and bureaucracies. And on the ground, an average developing country hosts no less than 23 different UN organizations. In the most vulnerable states, the number is even higher. We also have 10 human rights treaty bodies and 11 secretariats for global environmental treaties. I pay tribute to the dedicated and serious staff that is representing us all out there, in at times very difficult places. But those who care about the UN must ask: are we improving delivery, or just creating more fragmentation and duplication? The United Nations derives its legitimacy from the sovereign equality of states. Yet many Member States are struggling to keep pace and to participate. We must simplify. We must focus. We must improve our capacity to deliver as one and create more impact on the ground. We, the Member States, must give guidance to the Secretary-General in succeeding with the ongoing reform endeavor. At times, this might require a solid dose of tough love. President, the cost of war affects us all. Grain and fertilizer supplies disrupted by Russia's war against Ukraine undermine food security far beyond Europe's shores. Russia's war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz teach us the same lesson. When might succeeds over right, we all pay the price. Often, the consequences of war also come home to haunt the aggressor. What was described by President Putin as a special military operation that would be over in days or maybe weeks is now well into its fifth year. Likewise, there is no end in sight for the war in the Gulf. Both wars reminds us about the limitations of military power. Military action is never the goal in itself. Clausewitz described war as the continuation of politics by other means. Well, if the war's political goals cannot be achieved, war just becomes unnecessary death, destruction, and loss, and frankly, demonstrations of weakness. The limited success of these and other ongoing wars is in itself a strong argument for prevention, mediation, and peacebuilding. Diplomacy can work if we allow it to. We saw a good example of this this week. The agreement between our neighbor Denmark, Greenland and the United States serves an example of how good diplomacy can lead to a lasting solution that respects the interests of all parties while fully respecting their sovereign rights. Colleagues, we need to continue our quest to ensure that there can be no impunity for committing the most grave international crimes. The International Criminal Court is one of the most important expressions of this noble quest. Together with so many like-minded countries, we will strengthen our resolve to defend and to further develop the ICC. Norway resoundingly rejects the calls for dismantling the International Criminal Court. President, the triple crisis I have set out here is no less than an existential crisis for our United Nations. Yet, thankfully, to counter this, we have concrete proposals for reform on the table, the UN80 initiative. The UN80 initiative is a test of our ability to build a stronger, more robust UN. Norway supports the level of ambition that the Secretary-General has set out. We support the proposals across all work streams, including structural changes. The UN80 process has already produced successes. The mandate resolution laid the foundation for better joint decisions. We all agree that we must rationalize mandates, streamline reporting, and organize our work to allow for broad, effective participation. Norway is proud to play a role in this process. But we also do need structural change. We need to be better at delivering as one. Some UN organizations frankly overlap. They should be merged in order to serve our common interest. But unfortunately, colleagues, too often member states show vested interests, engage themselves in turf battles, and become fearful of change. Let me be clear, reform will not succeed if we always keep protecting the status quo. Let us remind ourselves that we, the Member States, are the owners of this organization, not the Secretariat. With that comes responsibility. The UN80 process needs to continue under the next Secretary-General. We need to see this initiative succeed. For an organization of 193 states to function, we need a strong, independent Secretary-General that firmly advocates the principles of the UN Charter with integrity and with authority. In a time of geopolitical tension, the Secretary-General's good offices function becomes more important than ever before. The next Secretary-General will face the formidable task of helping us lead the United Nations out of its current crisis. We need someone bold and transformative. She must be able to build trust to implement our decisions, lead meaningful reform, and improve effectiveness. A true reform of this organization must also address the composition and functioning of the Security Council. That is the common call of the majority of this room. The absence of Africa among the permanent seats of the Council is but one striking example. While striving to improve legitimacy, we must ensure that we do not reduce efficiency. We need a Security Council that is open, transparent and accountable in its deliberation. A Security Council that is both legitimate and effective, measured in its ability to take meaningful action. President, there is no lack of challenges to be tackled. While wars and geopolitical tensions dominate the agenda, we must not lose sight of our most important shared responsibility, which is to take better care of the planet on which we all depend. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and rampant pollution threatens life, property, and prosperity everywhere. The catastrophic floods that struck the Himalayas last month is yet another stark reminder of the growing risk associated with climate change. The good news is that reducing emissions and ensuring a more responsible management of the world's natural resources is possible. We already have the insights and technologies to make this transition possible. And they are increasingly competitive from an economic perspective, as seen by the fast falling costs of renewable energy. But we can only succeed if we cooperate. We cannot put fences around our own climate, our own biosphere, or deal with the ills of our oceans on our own. President, we live in an era of artificial intelligence. As the Secretary General said it in his speech, the danger is not technology, the danger is technology without accountability. I agree. Colleagues, We should not panic, but we must be determined. There is nothing inevitable in this development. Artificial intelligence is developed by humans and must remain under human direction, oversight, and control. It is becoming an integral part of our infrastructure, a part of almost all aspects of society and economy. And as we have done so many times before, we must maximize the positive benefits of emerging technologies while curbing its darker potentials. This week, Finland and Norway are appealing to businesses, governments, and the UN alike to cooperate for responsible management of the opportunities and the risks of artificial intelligence. Defense of essential human values goes well beyond regulating technology. For decades, we saw a growth in democratic governance, respect for the rule of law, and respect for human rights. Sadly, this trend has now turned. Democratic backsliding, polarization, and weakening of our democratic shields challenges many of our past achievements. Increasing economic inequality in countries exacerbate this trend. We should take democratic backsliding very seriously. While this may seem to be a domestic concern, we know that the way states behave internationally reflects on their domestic politics. Authoritarian and exclusivist sentiments within member states will therefore also affect our capacity to address our shared concerns. President, the United Nations is one of humanity's greatest achievements, not because it created a perfect world, it did not, but because it helped spare us from a far worse fate. For 80 years, it has proved a space where nations can negotiate instead of fight, cooperate instead of confront, and build rules instead of yielding to raw power. The world we know today is safer, more prosperous, and more just because the United Nations exists. The founders of the United Nations had witnessed two world wars and a global economic collapse. They knew something we must never forget. When law gives way to force, everybody loses. When cooperation collapses, everybody pays. When institutions fail, chaos follows. They did not build the United Nations because they believed mankind was perfect. They built it because they understood mankind is not. They built it because they knew that without rules, without dialogue, without cooperation, history has a habit of repeating its darkest chapters. The responsibility is now ours. Not only the Secretary-General's. Ours. The United Nations belongs to the Member States. We decide whether it succeeds or fails. We decide whether reform advances or stalls. The time for reports has passed. The time for action is now. It is our turn to face the monsters of our time.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway. I now give the floor to His Excellency Carlos Ramiro Martinez Alvarado. Minister of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala.

Mr. President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, The international system that has guided our relations over recent decades is undergoing a profound transformation. Conflicts, geopolitical tensions, declining resources for development, and the fragmentation of spaces for dialogue are testing the principles that have guided coexistence among nations.

At the same time, democracy faces a twofold challenge: the resurgence of authoritarian tendencies that seek to undermine the will of the people, and the spread of organized criminal networks that infiltrate institutions, corrupt justice systems, capture economies and territories, and erode public trust. Transnational organised crime is more than just a threat to public security. It is a direct threat to democracy, the rule of law and the ability of our peoples to freely determine their future. Criminal networks do not recognise borders. They are linked through drug trafficking, trafficking in persons, illicit arms trafficking, smuggling, extortion, money laundering, environmental crime and other illicit economies. They exploit institutional weaknesses, inequality and a lack of opportunities. Wherever the state is weakened, these structures seek to replace it, intimidate it or bend it to serve private interests. In the face of these realities, the fundamental principles that must guide our collective action have lost none of their relevance: preserving peace, Combating hunger and poverty, ensuring equal rights and opportunities, strengthening justice, protecting our planet, and consolidating democratic institutions remain shared responsibilities. The Sustainable Development Goals continue to provide an essential roadmap. It is precisely at moments such as this that international law, multilateralism, and democracy show their worth. Law provides us with common rules. Multilateralism enables us to turn shared problems into concerted solutions. And democracy ensures that power comes from the people and is exercised for their well-being. I address this Assembly on behalf of Guatemala, a country that knows from its own experience the value of these tools. Our history has taught us that democracy, peace and respect for the law are not permanent achievements. They are built collectively and each generation must preserve them. A democracy rests on free elections, legitimate institutions, the separation of powers, freedom of expression, public participation, transparency and accountability. but it also requires independent and effective institutions committed to the Constitution, the law and the popular mandate. Public institutions must not serve criminal networks, private agendas, personal loyalties or political or economic interests that are at odds with the common good. They must serve the people, the constitutional order and society's democratic interests. When an institution strays from that purpose, it does more than simply lose legitimacy. It weakens the democracy it is meant to protect. Democracy also earns its legitimacy in everyday life. When a family is protected from poverty, when a child learns in a decent school, when a woman lives free from violence, when a community is no longer isolated, and when a young person can envision a future without being forced to leave their country. That is why in Guatemala, we are restoring the state's capacity to reach those who have been excluded from opportunities for far too long. The intersectional Mano a Mano strategy brings together health, education, housing, nutrition, and community development to address poverty at the local level. Following crop losses caused by climate-related events, more than 450,000 families have received food assistance, while small-scale producers have gained access to seeds, tools, inputs, and insurance mechanisms. Public education is central to this effort. More than 1 million students have participated in initiatives to strengthen reading comprehension. We have expanded educational opportunities, promoted scholarships, strengthened instruction in national languages, and accelerated the digital transformation of the school system. In health care, We have expanded and refurbished facilities, strengthened regional services, and made progress in the comprehensive treatment of chronic diseases and cancer. Alongside the revival of road projects and public works in historically underserved communities, the National Digital Connectivity Plan now provides internet service to 383 public entities. We have also strengthened early warning systems for earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, and volcano hazards. Restoring the legitimate presence of the state also means providing security in accordance with the law, strengthening prevention, protecting communities, and pursuing criminal networks rather than only their visible manifestations. It means improving investigations, institutional coordination, and the tracing of the financial flows that sustain illicit economies. Guatemala maintains that the Charter of the United Nations and international law must remain our common point of reference. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of states must be respected. Disputes must be settled by peaceful means. Human rights must be protected. International humanitarian law must be observed in all circumstances. And international obligations must be fulfilled. The law loses its ability to protect us when we accept its selective application. National and international institutions lose legitimacy when they depart from their mandates in response to pressure, calculations or particular interests. Their authority rests on independence, impartiality, transparency and respect for the law. There cannot be one rule for the powerful and another for the weak, nor can there be victims whose suffering outrages us and others whose suffering we choose to ignore. For countries such as Guatemala, international law does not constrain our sovereignty; it is one of its principal safeguards. Guatemala believes in the peaceful settlement of disputes. We place our trust in dialogue, negotiation and the mechanisms provided for under international law, because even the most complex historical differences can and must be resolved by peaceful means. We are deeply concerned by the persistence of armed conflicts in different regions of the world and their devastating consequences for civilians. In every case, our position rests on the same principles: respect for the Charter and international law, the protection of civilians, safe humanitarian access, and dialogue and diplomacy as indispensable paths towards a just, sustainable and lasting peace. We must not grow accustomed to war. We must not accept violence as a permanent condition of our time or allow entire generations to grow up believing that force is the only way to resolve our differences. Guatemala stands for peace. This December, we will mark 30 years since the signing of the Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace, which brought an end to 36 years of internal armed conflict. After years of negotiation, we chose to replace armed violence with the pursuit of dialogue. That is why we understand the value of international support and the role of the United Nations. Our experience allows us to share one conviction. Negotiation is not a sign of weakness. Dialogue does not mean abandoning our principles. Seeking peace must never mean accepting injustice. We have also contributed to United Nations peacekeeping operations. More than 6,300 Guatemalan women and men have served under the United Nations flag in peacekeeping operations in different parts of the world. A country that knows the cost of war must also take responsibility for helping others preserve peace. Mr. President, we must strengthen the timely exchange of information operational and judicial coordination, border security with respect for human rights, the protection of ports and transit routes, financial and asset investigations, and the recovery of assets derived from illicit activities. We must also work together on prevention. Lasting security cannot be achieved through law enforcement alone. It requires education, decent work, resilient communities, accessible institutions and opportunities for young people. It requires us to reduce the social, territorial and economic spaces that criminal structures exploit to recruit, exert control and supplant the state. Our regional cooperation must be grounded in trust, shared responsibility and respect for sovereignty. It must not serve private agendas or become an instrument of interests alien to our peoples. Climate change, pandemics, transnational organized crime, food insecurity, human mobility and technological transformation all demand cooperation. Guatemala. A country particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change knows that adaptation, risk management and the protection of rural livelihoods require national efforts, but also financing and cooperation commensurate with the needs, capable of building capacity and delivering results. Defending multilateralism does not mean defending the status quo. The United Nations must become more effective, representative, transparent and responsive to people. It must make better use of its resources, reduce duplication and respond more swiftly without weakening the purposes for which it was created. Efficiency must strengthen, not erode, its three pillars: peace and security, sustainable development and human rights. Effectiveness cannot be measured solely in administrative terms, but rather by the ability to prevent a war, protect a population under threat, combat hunger, confront transnational criminal networks, or support a state in strengthening its institutions. We do not need a United Nations that is smaller in purpose. We need a United Nations that is stronger in results and firmer in defending democratic principles. That transformation must also reach the Security Council. Its composition must better reflect the realities of the 21st century and remedy the long-standing underrepresentation of entire regions. When the veto causes paralysis in the face of serious threats to international peace and security, confidence in the entire system suffers. We also face an important decision for the future of the organization, the selection of the next Secretary-General. Guatemala hopes that the process will be transparent and inclusive and will identify an independent leader able to build bridges, defend the principles of the Charter, and lead the reform our organization needs. The Latin American and Caribbean region stands ready and prepared to shoulder its responsibility to the international community. The time has come for a Latin American woman to serve as Secretary-General of the United Nations. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the Republic of Guatemala reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes and the observance of international law. We welcome the fact that the International Court of Justice has set the date for the oral hearings concerning the territorial, insular and maritime dispute with Belize. For my country, this is more than a procedural milestone. With the notification of the hearings, the final procedural stage before the Court delivers its judgment has begun. It marks the culmination of a legal dispute that has accompanied the people of Guatemala and successive governments since independence, and whose conclusion we eagerly await. We recognize that the Court's judgment, once delivered, will bring the dispute to an end. and we trust that it will provide legal certainty to both parties and lay the foundations for a new chapter in relations between Guatemala and Belize. In closing, I wish to say that Guatemala will continue to do its part, strengthening democratic institutions capable of meeting the needs of our people, resolutely confronting transnational organized crime and those who seek to capture institutions, defending international law consistently, promoting regional responses based on shared responsibility, and working for a United Nations capable of transforming itself to fulfil the promise contained in the opening words of our Charter: "We, the Peoples". restoring trust will depend on our ability to show that even in times of uncertainty and division, we remain capable of building together solutions that none of us could achieve alone. Thank you very much.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Guatemala. I now give the floor to Her Excellency Maria Malma Stengard, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Sweden.

Mr. President, Excellencies, I want to tell you about my grandmother Alice. Growing up in rural Sweden as the seventh of 11 siblings, her opportunities were very different from those of her brothers. Her parents expected her to focus first and foremost on family life, yet she was curious, capable and determined to build a life of her own. A job at a local bank gave her not only an income, but also independence and confidence. There at the bank, she met many women with little to no experience with finances and who were left vulnerable when circumstances changed. She wrote in her diary about some of the women she met, many of whom were recently widowed. coming to the bank in tears because they didn't know anything about their own family finances. One woman came to the bank holding two safe deposit keys without knowing which bank they belonged to. My grandmother was as independent as a woman in that time and place could be, but she worried deeply about the consequences for the women who were not. During her life, she witnessed extraordinary progress, but two generations later, far too many women are still entirely economically dependent on men. Mr. President, 80 years ago, when Sweden joined the United Nations, the foundations of our modern society were being laid. In the 1940s and 50s, Swedish women joined the labor market in large numbers. This was not only a matter of principle. It also came from the realization that our economy needed women in the workforce. Women's economic empowerment is a matter of freedom. When women work and earn their own money, their self-determination grows. Gender equality is not only the right thing to do, it's also the smart thing to do. When women work, economies grow. Mr. President, each generation must fight for equality. In 1919, the same year my grandmother was born, Sweden decided that women should have the right to vote. That very same year, women in Afghanistan were also granted the right to vote. More than a century later, the contrast between women's freedoms in our two countries is as striking as it is saddening. It is a painful reminder that progress is never irreversible. Rights once gained can be lost. Freedoms do not defend themselves. It is up to us to protect them for women and girls everywhere and for generations to come. Mr. President, when Sweden joined the UN in 1946, the world was emerging from the devastation of war. The lesson from that catastrophe was clear. Peace must not be taken for granted. Defense of sovereignty and territorial integrity has been at the heart of Swedish foreign policy ever since. Eight decades later, these principles are once again being challenged. Bad faith, conflict and utter contempt for the common rules are weakening the institutions that we built together. These are times of upheaval. The number of armed conflicts is growing, and civilians are paying the price. In Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Palestine, Lebanon, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and many other conflict zones, millions are suffering. Mr. President, Russia's aggression against Ukraine is a blatant violation of international law. It strikes at the heart of the very principles upon which the United Nations was founded. Sweden's support for Ukraine is felt deeply throughout our entire society. It comes from our people, our civil society, and the business community. We will support Ukraine for as long as it takes. Russia has not only violated the UN Charter, it has repeatedly violated international humanitarian law and human rights law. Attacks targeting civilians, forcible transfer of and deportation of children, conflict-related sexual violence and torture. The list is far too long. Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial. If there is anything that we have learned from history, It is that there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability. Sweden stands firmly behind the ICC, its independence and integrity, and recognizes its vital role, not least in Ukraine. Russia must also be held accountable for its breaches of the Chemical Weapons Convention, both on and off the battlefield. Russia's war of aggression against a peaceful neighbor is one of the biggest strategic mistakes and moral failures of the 21st century. Four and a half years after launching its full-scale invasion, Russia has failed to achieve its objectives. Its economy is under strain, and its casualty numbers are devastating. Ordinary Russians are withdrawing their funds from the bank, and a substantial share of Russia's young people are dying on the front lines. The impact of Russia's war of aggression extends far beyond Ukraine. Russia intensified its systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure and on vessels in the Black Sea this summer. This has once again disrupted global food supply chains, exacerbating an already dire situation for vulnerable people across the globe. To President Putin and Mr. Lavrov, I say this: the path to peace is clear. The choice should be easy. Withdraw your troops. End this war. Mr. President, Sweden has been an active contributor to the United Nations for 80 years, and we remain committed. But as a staunch partner, we will continue to push for a UN that is more effective, more transparent, and better equipped to uphold the principles of its Charter, a UN that is resolute. Sweden's first peacekeepers, 300 of them, served this organization during the Suez Crisis in 1956. Since then, more than 80,000 Swedes have followed in their footsteps. We have a long tradition of supporting mediation through the UN. It began in 1948 with UN's first mediator, Sweden's Folke Bernadotte. We have long been a major donor of development assistance, and we remain devoted to tackling global development challenges and contributing to urgent humanitarian efforts. Sweden remains a generous donor, but development assistance alone will not be enough to meet the challenges before us. Mr. President, reducing emissions to curb climate change is a common and global challenge and is necessary to safeguard and increase development gains in the coming decades. Sweden will continue to promote climate action based on urgency and opportunity. Urgency based on what science tells us, opportunity based on the economic growth, jobs, and strengthened competitiveness that climate transition brings. Given the state of the world, changes are necessary to ensure the UN's central role in international affairs and its ability to address today's challenges. An efficient, effective, nimble and well-coordinated UN is urgently needed. Sweden strongly supports the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative and expects all UN entities to engage fully, with a clear focus on improving delivery at country level. We also expect Member States to give the UN adequate resources. Assessed contributions must be paid in full and in time. As members, we also need to carefully consider institutional reforms and align mandates with available resources. UNAD is an opportunity to strengthen the UN's impact across all three pillars and to reinforce the international system, firmly grounded in the UN Charter of International Law. Sweden remains firm in its defense of the UN's normative mandates on human rights, gender equality, and sexual and reproductive health and rights. Everyone has the right to live freely and with dignity, to be who they are, and to love whom they choose. Sweden will always stand up for that freedom and for equal rights of all. Mr. President, a balanced expansion of the Security Council would strengthen its credibility and the legitimacy of its decisions. Sweden would like to see permanent and non-permanent seats added and a fairer representation of all continents on the Council. Africa, home to 1.3 billion people and the largest regional bloc in the United Nations, has no permanent seat. This is neither logical nor fair. Further, the veto should never be used to prevent the UN from acting against serious violations of international law or in humanitarian disasters. Mr. President, we must continue to strengthen our United Nations to make the organization stronger and better equipped to prevent conflict and meet the challenges of tomorrow. We must continue to find common agreements based on the fundamentals: every country's sovereignty and territorial integrity, prohibition of the use of force, respect for international law, human rights and humanitarian principles. It is our shared responsibility to ensure that the UN remains relevant, effective and resolute, that it becomes greater than the sum of its parts. to show once again that we can turn the page on conflict and chaos and move towards peace and prosperity. Mr. President, this year also marks 65 years since Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold died. His integrity, conviction and commitment to the vision and values of our organization are still remembered. Sweden continues to support the UN investigation aimed at clarifying the circumstances surrounding Secretary General Hammacher's death. And I would like to conclude with the words of Mr. Hammacher. It is no news to anybody But we sense it in different degrees that the world of today is more than ever before one world. The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one, not the military strength, the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of the people is indirectly the strength of all. Thank you.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Sweden. And I'll give the floor to his excellency Robert Komlan Edo Dusey. Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration, and Togolese Abroad of Togo.

Excellence.

Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, heads of state and government, President of the General Assembly, Secretary General, ladies and gentlemen, heads of delegations, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of the President of the Council, His Excellency Faure Essofima Gnassingbe, of the Government and the Togolese people, I would like, Mr. President, to convey to you my sincere and warm congratulations on your election to the presidency of this session of the General Assembly. To you, Secretary-General, Sir, and Mr. Antonio Guterres, I would like to convey Togo's sincere gratitude for your unfailing commitment to peace, to security, to solidarity, and to sustainable development. At a time when you are completing your term, Togo would like to pay a particular tribute to you for these years of commitment, of courage, of listening and of service for the defense of the ideals of the United Nations and to reform our organization. We would like to express the desire that the legacy of your action will continue to inspire our organization and to guide those people who will have the responsibility to continue your work. We wish you every success in the future for your future commitments. Mr. President, the topic of this section asks us to do two things: to be clear in our diagnosis and to be strong in our commitment. To be clear, because we can no longer have insufficient responses to those challenges that affect our international system. Commitment, because noting the limits of multilateralism should no longer mean that we renounce multilateralism. We need even more multilateralism and even more UN, a stronger UN in defending its principles more effective in preventing and peacefully settling disputes, more representative in its decision-making structures, and closer to the realities of the people. The world needs a UN that strengthens and re-establishes trust, a UN that listens without turning away from the concerns of those people that it serves, who decide without losing sight of those for whom it works and which promises without forgetting that it needs to keep its promises. International trust cannot be restored just through speeches. It is established through the respect of shared rules, and here we're talking about international law. Unfortunately, we are seeing a worsening of geopolitical tensions and a worrisome return to war at the heart of international relations. Violations of international law and of the United Nations Charter are increasing in number. And the weakness of our responses are akin to a type of tolerance that we seem to be willing to accept. Given this situation, Togo would like to reaffirm its firm belief international law is not an obstacle to power. It guarantees its legitimacy, its predictability, and its stability. It protects the most vulnerable states, and also serves the lasting interests of the most powerful by preventing uncontrolled clashes, by shoring up exchanges, and by establishing trust. Togo thus defends a pragmatic type of multilateralism that transforms commitments into results that scaffolds power dynamics with shared rules and organizes the peaceful coexistence of interests. Mr. President, Togo supports efforts as part of the UN80 initiative to improve the effectiveness, the coherence and the accountability of our organization. Mr. President, economic and climate vulnerabilities are having an impact on stability and security. In Africa, these are coupled with ongoing security challenges and can fuel tensions and conflict. This is why development questions, questions of peace and security must be tackled in a complementary and interlinked fashion. Lasting security cannot be boiled down just to its military dimension. It requires us to act on factors causing vulnerability and it requires us to promote dialogue, prevention and mediation. Along these lines, the President of the Council, His Excellency Faure Essozima Gnassingbe, has striven to promote dialogue, to bring people's positions closer and to contribute to find political solutions to crises that affect regions. In West Africa and in the Sahel, for example, our country is working hard to encourage exchanges and to contribute to the emergence of lasting political responses. In the Great Lakes region, Togo, as part of African mediation, is also making its contribution to de-escalation, to restoring trust, and to the quest for lasting responses to disputes. These initiatives reflect a conviction. In the face of crises, we need to maintain spaces for dialogue. We need to foster political and diplomatic means. Mediation is not a weakness. It is an expression of responsibility. Togo has made dialogue and preventive diplomacy the pillars of its foreign policy. In our West African sub-region and at the African level, Togo is working unfailingly to promote mediation, stability and the peaceful settlement of disputes. We are convinced that no lasting solution can be imposed from the outside without actively listening to local and sovereign realities and what's going on on the ground. Africa is not asking for others to act in its place. It is asking for its efforts to be recognized, assisted and supported. Mr. President, On the 26th of September 2025, almost to the day a year ago, right here before this august assembly, I challenged the universal conscience on the distortion of the map of the world which wrongly shrunk the size of Africa on the map of the world and in the global collective imagination. Just a few days ago, on the 4th of September 2026 to be precise, in this very hall, Togo's call was heard and a reform of the map of the world was adopted. The international community made history by adopting, with a very large majority of 164 votes, by adopting a resolution called "Correct the Map". Togo is delighted that this resolution was adopted. This decision has a simple requirement, is it? The need to represent the world based on scientific truth and respecting the equal dignity of the people. Correcting the map is not just rectifying a geographical distortion. It's also correcting the perceptions that come with, in particular in education, in information and in public action. Correcting the map of the world on behalf of scientific truth, on behalf of responsibility in the face of history, on behalf of justice and equity, on behalf of repairing cartographic map distortions that were inherited from the past in English.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of this resolution is not the end of our journey. The adoption of this resolution is now the beginning of our resolution. For us, As African, the adoption of this resolution is far more than a cartographic decision. The adoption of this resolution is an act of recognition. The adoption of this resolution is an act of reparation. The adoption of this resolution, it's an act of justice. The adoption of this resolution is for justice in the world. That way, today, we have not redrawn the world. We have corrected the way in which the world is represented. Togo intends to build on this historic momentum. We count on the continued mobilization of Member States of the United Nations and its agencies, of regional organizations, of scientific institutions and of technology platforms to translate this resolution into concrete action. Because a resolution must not remain a text. Resolution must become action. Action must become knowledge. Knowledge must become education. And education must become understanding among peoples. As we say, a fairer map does not redraw the border of the world. It transforms the way we see the world ourself. Togo now wishes to move from resolution to action. We propose the opening of a new phase of international cooperation, bringing together the member state, the agency of United Nation, we say scientific and academic institution, geographer and cartographers, historian, educators, young people, and the innovators shaping the technologies of tomorrow, including artificial intelligence. Our objective is clear, dear friends, to make cartography an even more powerful instrument of knowledge, education, inclusion, and mutual understanding amongst people. We must encourage research We must develop also a new education tools for our generation. Excellencies, the digital revolution give us the issue and in turn a new dimension. Billion of people now consult maps every day on their phones, their computers and digital platform. Children, for example, discover the world through the digital maps. The businessmen make decision using cartographic data. The government also rely on special information and artificial intelligence system increasingly interpret our planet through digital data and cartographic representation. The question before us. Therefore, it's no longer only about printed maps. It's about the digital image of our planet that we are transmitting to the generation of tomorrow. Ladies and gentlemen, we also want Correct the Map to become a dialogue between generations. We want young people to have the opportunity to look at our planet with a fresh eyes. We want schools, universities, and research institution to become places where the representation of our world can be studied, questioned, and understood. We want African cartographers to contribute We want European cartographers to contribute. We want Asian cartographers to contribute. We want cartographers from America, from Arab region, Pacific, and every region in the world to contribute, because the world belongs to all of us. And because the way we represent our world should be a conversation open to all. Excellencies, today, Togo launches an appeal, an appeal to all member states, an appeal to international organizations, an appeal to the scientific community, an appeal to educators, an appeal to innovators, an appeal to the young people of the world. Let us correct the map an international laboratory for reflection, refresh, and innovation on the representation of our world. Let us transform this resolution into a program of cooperation. Let us transform an idea into knowledge. Let us transform knowledge into education, and let us transform education into greater understanding among the people we serve. We know now what we have to do for our generation. We are not here simply to correct a map. We are here to help correct a way of seeing, a way of seeing some things inherited from the past, a way of seeing that can be enriched by science, A way of seeing that can be rebalanced by our knowledge. And ultimately, a way of seeing that reminds us of one simple truth. We share our planet. We share our humanity. And we must learn to see our common world with greater occurrence, greater justice, and greater understanding. Let us correct the map. Let us broaden our perspective. Let us strengthen our understanding.

Excellencies, the fact that a resolution called "Correct the Map" was adopted here on the 4th of September 2026 will go down in the history books. And we would like the history books to remember another thing, that thanks to this resolution, the United Nations begun a global dialogue on the way humanity represents itself. Togo stands ready to continue this dialogue. And finally, we invite all member states to join us. We invite scientists to guide us. We invite educators to support us. We invite youth to hold us to account. and we invite innovators to help us to build the tools of the future. Correct the map is not the end of the map. Correct the map is the beginning of a new way of seeing the world. Thank you for your kind attention.

I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration and Togolese Abroad of Togo. We have heard the last speaker in the general debate for this meeting. We will continue the general debate tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. in this hall. The exercise of the right of reply has been requested. I propose that the time limits for statements in the exercise of the right of reply under this item be limited to five minutes. for the first intervention and three minutes for the second intervention. Is there any objection to this proposal? I hear none. It is so decided. Accordingly, pursuant to rule 72 of the rules of procedure of the Assembly, when a representative exceeds her or his allotted time, The President shall call the speaker to order without delay, which will be done by means of automatic microphone cut-off. To assist delegations in managing their time, a countdown clock will be displayed on the screens. Members are also reminded that statements in the exercise of the right of reply should be made by delegations from their seats. I call on the representative of India.

Thank you, Mr. President. This afternoon, the General Assembly heard some bizarre remarks from the representative of Pakistan. This happens just a fortnight after New York City and the world marked the 25th anniversary of the horrendous 9/11 terrorist attack. This context, Mr. President, is important to keep in mind because its mastermind, Osama bin Laden, was living right on the doorstep of Pakistani Army's premier academy. And this was the very entity which was the subject of such deep genuflection before us today by the representative of Pakistan. But all this is only to be expected from what Pakistanis themselves call a Form 47 government. We heard some hypocritical homilies about democratic rights and human values from a regime whose capital at this very moment is being fortified against its own people. And that, Mr. President, is happening because this is a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army. Their puppets may come and go. But let us have no illusion who calls the shots. The reality of Pakistan is expressed in its 27th amendment and the lifelong immunity granted to its real ruler. Mr. President, the views we heard emanate from those with a long record of bigotry and hatred. They claim to uphold security during the day, they actually carry out terrorism at night. This Assembly was subjected to remarks about religious intolerance from the very regime whose mainstay is blasphemy laws. The world knows how minorities are treated in Pakistan. No pious platitude can mislead it. References were made to the Indian Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. This is an integral and inalienable part of my country and will always remain so. But if we must talk about Kashmir, let us turn our attention to the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Ask the people of Rawalpindi about the wanton killings, the brutal violence, and the denial of basic rights that they have long experienced. At the heart of the issue, Mr. President, is the longstanding practice of cross-border terrorism by Pakistan. We demonstrated last year that terrorists will have nowhere to run and nowhere to hide. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised, and continued terrorism by Pakistan will have consequences. It will understandably call into question what were premised on friendship and goodwill. We are confident that this Assembly will recognize Pakistan and its policies for what they really are. not what its representative mendaciously projects it to be. Reiterating falsehoods year after year does not make them true. Pakistan's terrorism, deceit, and duplicity will neither benefit it nor the world. I thank you, Mr. President.
I call on the representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. My delegation is compelled to respond to a state that has elevated propaganda into statecraft, embraced disinformation as diplomacy, exports terrorism as an instrument of policy, pursues hegemony as a regional strategy, mainstreams Islamophobia and Hindutva ideology. Let me present the extraordinary balance sheet of today's incredibly intolerant India. It exports terrorism and violence while trying to import victimhood and sympathy. Pakistan knows the cost of Indian-sponsored terrorism all too well. Since the turn of the century, Pakistan has lost nearly 100,000 lives to terrorism, generations scarred and billions of dollars drained from our economy. Pakistan's counter-terrorism efforts and sacrifices have been well recognized by the international community. We have also presented the international community extensive evidence of India's financing, aiding and abetting of terrorist groups targeting Pakistani civilians. including TTP, BLA and Majid Brigade. Yet, despite its endless lectures to others on terrorism, we are still awaiting to hear India unequivocally condemn the terrorist attacks that kill innocent Pakistani civilians. But how can we expect India to condemn its proxies? India's terrorist exports have gone from regional to global. From a serving Indian naval commander, Kulbhushan Jadhav, convicted in Pakistan on terrorism and espionage charges, to Nikul Gupta, who pleaded guilty in the United States for plotting murder of a Sikh leader at the hands of its government, and other implicated in assassination carried out in Canada, India's record speaks for itself. Turning over to the Jammu and Kashmir dispute, Jammu and Kashmir never was, neither is, nor will ever be integral part of India. It is an internationally recognized disputed territory, a huge part of which is under India's forcible and illegal occupation for nearly eight decades against the wishes of the Kashmiri people and in gross violation of international law and numerous resolutions of the Security Council. The contrast between Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir could not be more stark. In AJK, Kashmiris enjoy rights, participate in political life, and have the freedom to express their opinions, while in occupied Kashmir, they endure decades of occupation, repression, and denial of their fundamental right, including their right to self-determination. Rights cannot be equated with rights denied. Mr. President, the ruling RSS-BJP dispensation in India has institutionalized Hindutva ideology in state policy and practice and unleashed a reign of terror against minorities. Muslims are demonized, Christians persecuted, Dalits dehumanized, and Sikhs disenfranchised in the largest hypocrisy of the world.
